chunk.title: MUTCD: what it is and which edition is current
chunk.topic: Traffic control: MUTCD basics and status
chunk.text: The MUTCD (Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices) is the national standard for signs, cones, flaggers and every other traffic control device on roads open to the public. Part 6 covers temporary traffic control: construction, utility work, maintenance and incidents. The current edition is the 11th Edition, dated December 2023 and effective January 18, 2024. FHWA issued Revision 1 (dated December 2025) by a final rule effective March 5, 2026; it makes technical and editorial corrections, and the key Part 6 tables (sign spacing, tapers, stopping sight distance) read the same in Revision 1. States had two years, to January 18, 2026, to adopt the 11th Edition, either as is, with a state supplement, or as their own state manual that substantially conforms. The 11th Edition renumbered Part 6: flaggers are now Chapter 6D, tapers are Section 6B.08, and the typical applications are Chapter 6P (TA-1 to TA-54). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition Part 6; FHWA final rule 91 FR (Mar. 5, 2026), FR Doc. 2026-04365; 23 CFR 655.601(d)(2)(i), 655.603(b)(3)

chunk.title: MUTCD: how a state adopts it and whose manual wins
chunk.topic: Traffic control: MUTCD basics and status
chunk.text: Federal rule 23 CFR 655.603 makes the MUTCD the national standard for all traffic control devices on streets and highways open to public travel. A state may use the national manual as is, add a state supplement, or publish its own state MUTCD, but the state document has to be in substantial conformance: at a minimum it keeps the national Standard statements. States must adopt FHWA changes within two years of the final rule's effective date. That is why the 11th Edition (effective January 18, 2024) had a January 18, 2026 state deadline, and Revision 1 (effective March 5, 2026) gives states until March 5, 2028 by the same two-year rule. On the job, the order is: the approved traffic control plan or permit for that road, then the state's manual or supplement and DOT standard plans, then the national MUTCD. A city or county can be stricter than the state. If you do not know which edition your state is on, ask the agency that issued the permit.
chunk.source: 23 CFR 655.603(a), (b)(1)-(3); FHWA final rule FR Doc. 2026-04365 (effective Mar. 5, 2026); MUTCD state information page

chunk.title: MUTCD: what Standard, Guidance, Option and Support mean
chunk.topic: Traffic control: MUTCD basics and status
chunk.text: Every paragraph in the MUTCD is labeled. Standard means required: it uses the word shall, and you do not deviate without an engineering study where the manual allows one. Guidance means recommended practice: it uses should, and you follow it unless engineering judgment says otherwise. Option means allowed: it uses may. Support is background only. This matters when a crew asks if something is the law. Examples from Part 6: high-visibility apparel for workers in the right-of-way is a Standard (Section 6C.05); lighting flagger stations at night is a Standard (Section 6D.06); taper lengths (Section 6B.08) and cone spacing (Section 6K.01) are Guidance; using Table 6B-2 distances for a buffer space is an Option. The typical application drawings in Chapter 6P are generally treated as Guidance, except the notes that are labeled Standard. A state manual can turn national Guidance into a state Standard. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6P.01 para. 2, 6C.05, 6D.06, 6B.08, 6K.01, 6B.06
chunk.note: Definitions of the four labels are in MUTCD Part 1, not re-read on 2026-11-20; the Part 6 examples were read.

chunk.title: Traffic control plan (TCP): when you need one, and work zone speed limit drops
chunk.topic: Traffic control: MUTCD basics and status
chunk.text: A temporary traffic control (TTC) plan describes the signs, devices and flagging used to move drivers, bikes and pedestrians through or around the work. The MUTCD says a plan should be developed for any planned work that affects road users, and planning should be finished before the site is occupied, even on minor jobs (Section 6B.01). The plan can be a detailed drawing or simply a reference to a typical application or the agency's standard plan. It should be prepared by someone knowledgeable (trained or certified) in traffic control, should keep an accessible route for pedestrians, and any change or alternate plan should be approved before it is used. The public agency with jurisdiction over the road is responsible for traffic control plans and devices (Section 6A.01), which is why the city, county or state permit decides what is approved. Speed limit reductions should be avoided where practical and kept to 10 mph or less; larger drops need a restrictive feature, extra notice and a step-down (Section 6B.01). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6A.01 para. 11, 6B.01 paras. 2-3, 5-11, 14, 17-20

chunk.title: Work zone parts: advance warning, transition, activity and termination areas
chunk.topic: Traffic control: parts of a work zone
chunk.text: A temporary traffic control zone has four parts (Section 6B.03). 1, Advance warning area: where drivers are told what is coming. It can be one sign or a vehicle with flashing lights, or a series of signs (Section 6B.04). 2, Transition area: where drivers are moved out of their normal path, usually with a taper of cones or drums. Except for mobile work, the redirect has to be made with channelizing devices or other traffic control devices (Section 6B.05, Standard). 3, Activity area: where the work happens. It holds the work space (closed to traffic, for workers, equipment and material), the traffic space (where traffic runs past) and the buffer space (empty separation) (Section 6B.06). 4, Termination area: where drivers return to their normal path, from the end of the work to the last device. An END ROAD WORK sign or a downstream taper may be used (Section 6B.07). The work zone runs from the first warning sign or flashing vehicle light to the END ROAD WORK sign or the last device (Section 6B.02). Set up in that order going with traffic and take down in reverse. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6B.02 to 6B.07

chunk.title: Buffer space: what it is, how long, and what cannot be in it
chunk.topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
chunk.text: The buffer space is empty road between traffic and the work space. It gives a driver who misses the taper room to stop before reaching the crew. A longitudinal buffer sits ahead of the work space; a lateral buffer sits beside it, next to an open trench, a drop-off or opposing traffic. The MUTCD says no work, and no storage of equipment, vehicles or material, should be in a buffer space (Section 6B.06, Guidance). If a truck with an attenuator, an arrow board or a message sign sits in the closed lane, only the part upstream of it counts as buffer. The width of a lateral buffer is set by engineering judgment. For the length of a longitudinal buffer the manual lets you use the stopping sight distances in Table 6B-2: 20 mph 115 ft, 25 mph 155 ft, 30 mph 200 ft, 35 mph 250 ft, 40 mph 305 ft, 45 mph 360 ft, 50 mph 425 ft, 55 mph 495 ft, 60 mph 570 ft, 65 mph 645 ft, 70 mph 730 ft, 75 mph 820 ft. Use the posted speed, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work started, or the expected operating speed. The same table may be used to place a flagger station. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6B.06 paras. 6-15; Table 6B-2; Section 6D.06 para. 3

chunk.title: Taper length formulas: L = WS squared / 60 and L = WS
chunk.topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
chunk.text: Taper length L in feet comes from Table 6B-4. For 40 mph or less: L = W x S x S / 60. For 45 mph or more: L = W x S. W is the width of the offset in feet (how far traffic is moved sideways, usually the lane width). S is the posted speed limit, or the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed, in mph. Table 6B-3 then sets the length by type of taper. Merging taper (closing a lane where traffic has to merge): at least L. Shifting taper (moving traffic sideways with no merge): at least 1/2 L. Shoulder taper (closing a shoulder): at least 1/3 L. One-lane, two-way traffic taper (the short taper in front of a flagger): 50 ft minimum, 100 ft maximum. Downstream taper (end of the work space): 50 ft minimum, 100 ft maximum. In the one-lane two-way taper and the downstream taper the devices go about 20 ft apart. A 12 ft lane at 35 mph: 12 x 35 x 35 / 60 = 245 ft. A 12 ft lane at 55 mph: 12 x 55 = 660 ft. Longer is not always better: in town, short blocks and driveways can make a long taper worse (Section 6B.08). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6B.08 paras. 3-14; Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4

chunk.title: Taper lengths worked out by speed for 10, 11 and 12 ft lanes
chunk.topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
chunk.text: Merging taper lengths from the MUTCD formulas in Table 6B-4 (L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less, L = W x S at 45 mph or more), worked out here, in feet. 12 ft lane: 20 mph 80, 25 mph 125, 30 mph 180, 35 mph 245, 40 mph 320, 45 mph 540, 50 mph 600, 55 mph 660, 60 mph 720, 65 mph 780, 70 mph 840. 11 ft lane: 25 mph 115, 30 mph 165, 35 mph 225, 40 mph 293, 45 mph 495, 55 mph 605, 65 mph 715. 10 ft lane: 25 mph 104, 30 mph 150, 35 mph 204, 40 mph 267, 45 mph 450, 55 mph 550, 65 mph 650. A shifting taper is half of these. A shoulder taper is one third, using the shoulder width as W: an 8 ft shoulder at 45 mph is 8 x 45 / 3 = 120 ft, and at 55 mph 147 ft. Notice the jump between 40 and 45 mph, where the formula changes: a 12 ft lane goes from 320 ft to 540 ft. These are minimums from the national formula; round up, and use your state's table if it has one. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4 (lengths computed from the formulas, not printed in the MUTCD)
chunk.note: Computed values; the 12 ft column matches California MUTCD 2026 Table 6B-3(CA).

chunk.title: Worked example: closing one lane for a utility job on a 35 mph street
chunk.topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
chunk.text: Example using the national MUTCD numbers for a 12 ft lane closed on a multi-lane 35 mph city street. Merging taper: L = 12 x 35 x 35 / 60 = 245 ft (Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4). Cones in the taper no more than 35 ft apart, which is 8 cones for 245 ft; cones along the work space no more than 70 ft apart (Section 6K.01). Buffer space ahead of the work, if used: 250 ft at 35 mph (Table 6B-2), kept empty. Downstream taper: 50 to 100 ft with cones about 20 ft apart (Section 6B.08). Advance signs: three signs. If the agency treats the street as urban low speed they are at least 100 ft apart; as urban high speed, 350 ft apart (Table 6B-1). ROAD WORK AHEAD or UTILITY WORK AHEAD comes first, then the lane closed sign, then the lane ends sign. At night the cones must be at least 28 inches tall with reflective bands (Section 6K.03). Same job at 45 mph: taper 540 ft, cones 45 ft apart in the taper and 90 ft along the work, buffer 360 ft. This is arithmetic from the national manual, not an approved plan. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Tables 6B-1, 6B-2, 6B-3, 6B-4; Sections 6B.08, 6K.01, 6K.03, 6H.24

chunk.title: Sidewalk closed: what you owe pedestrians
chunk.topic: Traffic control: pedestrians and sidewalks
chunk.text: If the work zone affects where people walk, adequate pedestrian access and walkways shall be provided (Section 6C.02, Standard). Tell people before they reach the closure, and send them across at an intersection, not mid-block, so nobody walks up to a dead end. A good temporary route does three things: no conflict with the work or equipment, no conflict with traffic moving around the site, and a convenient, accessible path that is close to what the sidewalk was. Do not take the pedestrian route away just to park trucks or store material. Tape, rope and plastic chain should not be used to control pedestrians because a person using a cane cannot detect them. Keep truck and equipment crossings of the walkway to a minimum and use a flagger when they cross. Where the walkway is close to traffic, separate it with temporary traffic barrier; normal curb does not count as a barrier. Signs: SIDEWALK CLOSED (R9-9) at the closure, SIDEWALK CLOSED USE OTHER SIDE (R9-10), and SIDEWALK CLOSED AHEAD CROSS HERE (R9-11) at the crossing before it. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6C.02 paras. 2-9, 14-17, 20, 23, 28; Section 6G.10

chunk.title: Temporary pedestrian route: ADA numbers (width, ramps, edging)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: pedestrians and sidewalks
chunk.text: When a sidewalk or crosswalk is closed or moved, the temporary route shall be detectable and have accessibility features consistent with the route it replaces, and a barrier that a long cane can detect shall span the full width of the closed sidewalk (Section 6C.03, Standard). Numbers from Part 6: keep the existing width where practical; 60 inches is the target, and where that cannot be held provide a 60 by 60 inch passing space at least every 200 ft (Section 6C.02). The sidewalk detour drawing (TA-28) allows a 48 inch route with a 60 inch passing area every 200 ft. Temporary ramps: slope 12:1 (8.33 percent) or flatter, slip-resistant, with a landing at least 48 by 48 inches and cross-slope 2 percent or flatter (TA-28, Standard). Surface: smooth, hard, no abrupt grade changes. Detectable edging along a channelized route: top at least 8 inches above the walk, bottom no more than 2 inches above it, continuous (Section 6M.04). Pedestrian channelizing devices: hand-trailing edge 32 to 38 inches high (Section 6K.02). Printed signs do not help a blind pedestrian; a continuous detectable barrier does. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6C.02 para. 11, 6C.03 paras. 4-6, 6K.02 para. 8, 6M.04 para. 2; Figure 6P-28 (TA-28) notes 1, 2, 14

chunk.title: Worker safety in a work zone: what the MUTCD says to plan for
chunk.topic: Traffic control: parts of a work zone
chunk.text: Section 6C.04 lists the things that should be considered to protect workers. Training: all workers should be trained to work next to traffic in a way that lowers their exposure, and workers with traffic control duties trained in the devices. Temporary traffic barrier along the work space, depending on how close traffic is, its speed, how long the job lasts, the time of day and the volume. Speed reduction: speed zoning, funneling, lane reduction, law enforcement or flaggers. Activity area planned so backing of trucks and equipment is kept to a minimum. Worker safety planning: a trained person does a basic hazard assessment of the site and the job classifications (the manual points to the OSHA General Duty Clause and 29 CFR 1926.20(b)(2)). Extras that may be used: a shadow vehicle with a truck-mounted attenuator, closing the road and detouring traffic, police presence on short risky jobs, lighting for night work, and special devices such as rumble strips, message signs, warning lights or intrusion alarms. The section warns that overusing special devices makes drivers stop noticing them. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6C.04 paras. 1-5

chunk.title: High-visibility vest: what class the MUTCD requires
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: All workers within the right-of-way who are inside the work zone, flaggers and emergency responders included, shall wear high-visibility safety apparel that meets Performance Class 2 or 3 of ANSI/ISEA 107-2015 (Section 6C.05, Standard). A person the employer designates picks Class 2 or Class 3 for the job. Background material is fluorescent orange-red or fluorescent yellow-green, or both; the retroreflective material is orange, yellow, white, silver or yellow-green. Flaggers working at night should wear Class 3 (Guidance). Police directing traffic or working a closure wear it too; emergency and law enforcement personnel may wear an ANSI/ISEA 207-2006 public safety vest instead. OSHA has the same floor for trench crews: workers exposed to public vehicle traffic must wear warning vests or other reflective or high-visibility garments (29 CFR 1926.651(d)), and flagger garments must follow MUTCD Part 6 (29 CFR 1926.201(a)). Some states are stricter, for example on colors or on Class 3 for flaggers at all times. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6C.05 paras. 1-7; 29 CFR 1926.651(d); 29 CFR 1926.201(a)

chunk.title: Flagger training: what the national MUTCD says
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: The national MUTCD does not issue flagger cards. Section 6D.01 is Guidance: because flaggers are responsible for public safety and deal with the public more than any other worker, they should be trained in safe traffic control practices and public contact techniques. A flagger should be able to: receive and pass on specific instructions clearly, firmly and courteously; move fast enough to get out of the way of an errant vehicle; control the paddle or flag so drivers get clear guidance as conditions change; apply safe practices under stress or in an emergency; and recognize a dangerous traffic situation and warn the crew in time. The card or certification rule comes from the state: the state DOT specifications, the state MUTCD or supplement, or the state safety agency. Many states name the courses they accept and how long a card lasts (2, 3 or 4 years are common). OSHA ties in through 29 CFR 1926.201(a): flagger signaling and the use of flaggers must conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6D.01 para. 1 (Guidance); 29 CFR 1926.201(a)

chunk.title: Flagger equipment: STOP/SLOW paddle, flag size and flashlight
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: The STOP/SLOW paddle should be the primary and preferred hand-signaling device because it gives drivers clearer guidance than a red flag (Section 6D.02, Guidance). The paddle shall be an octagon on a rigid handle and shall be retroreflectorized when used at night (Standard). The STOP face is red with white letters and border; the SLOW face is orange with black letters and border. Lights may be added to the paddle; if they flash, the rate is 50 to 60 flashes a minute, with white or red lights on the STOP face and white or yellow on the SLOW face. Flags should be limited to emergencies (Section 6D.03). A flag shall be red or fluorescent orange-red, at least 24 inches square, fastened to a staff about 36 inches long, and retroreflectorized at night. In an emergency at night at a station that is not lit, a flashlight with a red glow cone may be added: flashlight in the left hand, paddle or flag in the right (Section 6D.04). The minimum paddle size is set in the figure and in state manuals; check your state's size. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6D.02 paras. 1-9, 6D.03 paras. 1-4, 6D.04 paras. 1-2
chunk.note: National minimum paddle width (18 in in earlier editions) was not confirmed from the 11th Edition text on 2026-11-20; left out on purpose.

chunk.title: Flagger signals: stop, proceed, slow
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: With the paddle (Section 6D.05, Standard). To stop traffic: face the drivers, hold the STOP face toward them with the arm straight out from the body, and raise the free hand with the palm toward traffic, above shoulder level. To let traffic go: turn the SLOW face toward the stopped drivers and wave them on with the free hand. To alert or slow traffic: hold the SLOW face toward traffic with the arm straight out; you may also move the free hand up and down, palm down. With a flag (emergencies): to stop, hold the staff straight out across the lane so the whole flag hangs below it, free palm raised; to let traffic go, lower the flag and arm out of sight and wave with the free hand, and never wave traffic on with the flag. Hand signals alone, with no paddle, flag or automated flagger device, shall not be used on a one-lane two-way operation. Where to stand: on the shoulder next to the lane you control, or in the closed lane, before traffic stops. Step into the lane only after the vehicles have stopped. Stay visible and stand alone. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6D.05 paras. 2-6; Figure 6D-1

chunk.title: Flagger station: where to put it and night lighting
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: A flagger station shall be placed so approaching drivers have enough distance to stop at the stopping point (Section 6D.06, Standard). The stopping sight distances in Table 6B-2 may be used: 25 mph 155 ft, 30 mph 200 ft, 35 mph 250 ft, 40 mph 305 ft, 45 mph 360 ft, 50 mph 425 ft, 55 mph 495 ft, 60 mph 570 ft, 65 mph 645 ft. Increase the distance on a downgrade. The station should be far enough ahead of the crew that a car that runs the stop can still stop before the work space, and the flagger should pick an escape route before starting. Except in an emergency, a flagger station shall have advance warning signs ahead of it, and shall be illuminated when flagging at night (Standard). A Flagger sign (W20-7 symbol or W20-7a word sign) should be used ahead of any flagger; a BE PREPARED TO STOP sign may be added and goes between the Flagger sign and the ONE LANE ROAD sign. On a curve or hill crest, lengthen the buffer so the flagger and the back of the line of stopped cars can be seen in time (TA-10). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6D.06 paras. 1-5; Table 6B-2; Section 6H.15; Figure 6P-10 (TA-10) notes 6-8

chunk.title: One lane, two-way traffic: flaggers, pilot car, signal or stop signs
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: When both directions have to share one lane for a short distance, movements from each end shall be coordinated (Section 6E.01, Standard). The ways to do it: flaggers, a flag transfer, a pilot car, a temporary traffic signal, or STOP or YIELD signs. Flagger method: a flagger at each end, one of them named the lead, talking by radio or by hand signals that cannot be mistaken for flagging signals. One flagger is allowed only if that flagger can see the whole zone, on a short, low-volume, straight job; the single flagger should stand on the shoulder opposite the work or where visibility is good (Section 6E.02). Flag transfer: the last driver in carries a red flag or token to the other flagger; only for short sections, usually no more than 1 mile (Section 6E.03). Pilot car: a PILOT CAR FOLLOW ME sign (G20-4) shall be on the vehicle and the operation shall be coordinated with the control at each end (Section 6E.04). STOP or YIELD control: only on low-volume roads where drivers can see the other end and oncoming traffic (Section 6E.06). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6E.01 to 6E.06

chunk.title: Work zone signs: mounting height, color and portable stands
chunk.topic: Traffic control: advance warning signs
chunk.text: Work zone warning signs are orange with black legend. Signs used at night shall be retroreflective or illuminated, and street lighting does not count as illumination (Section 6F.01, Standard). Put signs on the right side of the road unless the manual says otherwise. Height to the bottom of the sign: at least 5 ft at the side of a rural road; at least 7 ft in business, commercial or residential areas where parked cars or people would block the view, and at least 7 ft above a sidewalk. A sign on a barricade or portable stand shall be at least 1 ft above the traveled way. Signs on portable supports that do not reach the 5 or 7 ft heights should not be used for more than 3 days (Section 6F.02). Take signs down or cover them as soon as they no longer apply, including during a short stop in the work (Section 6A.03, Standard). Standard size for the diamond warning signs such as ROAD WORK AHEAD and the Flagger sign is 36 by 36 inches on conventional roads and 48 by 48 inches on freeways and expressways; the 30 by 30 inch minimum is only for low-volume rural roads, local streets and roads at 30 mph or less (Section 6F.01, Table 6H-1). The approved plan governs.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6F.01 paras. 2-12, 6F.02 paras. 1-11, 6A.03 para. 4; Table 6H-1

chunk.title: Which warning signs a utility crew uses, with sign numbers
chunk.topic: Traffic control: advance warning signs
chunk.text: Common Part 6 signs. ROAD WORK AHEAD (W20-1): the general warning and the first sign drivers should see; STREET may replace ROAD. UTILITY WORK AHEAD (W21-7): may be used instead of ROAD WORK for utility operations on or next to the road (Section 6H.24). Flagger symbol (W20-7) or FLAGGER word sign (W20-7a): ahead of any flagger. ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD (W20-4): for a one-lane two-way operation. BE PREPARED TO STOP (W3-4): optional, between the Flagger sign and ONE LANE ROAD. Lane closed signs (W20-5) and lane ends signs (W4-2): for a lane closure on a multi-lane road. SHOULDER WORK (W21-5) and RIGHT or LEFT SHOULDER CLOSED (W21-5a): shoulder work with the road open. Workers symbol (W21-1): workers in or near the road. STEEL PLATE AHEAD (W8-24): warns that temporary plates may be uneven and slippery when wet (Section 6H.28). END ROAD WORK (G20-2): near the downstream end; it may go on the back of a sign facing the other way. SIDEWALK CLOSED signs are R9-9, R9-10 and R9-11. Add a warning sign on any side street or busy driveway that enters inside the work zone (Section 6H.03). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.

chunk.title: Cone spacing: in the taper and along the work
chunk.topic: Traffic control: cones, drums, barricades and arrow boards
chunk.text: MUTCD Section 6K.01 (Guidance): the spacing between cones, tubular markers, vertical panels, drums or barricades should not be more than 1 times the speed limit in feet in a taper, and not more than 2 times the speed limit in feet along a tangent (the straight run beside the buffer and the work space). At 25 mph that is 25 ft in the taper and 50 ft along the work; at 35 mph, 35 ft and 70 ft; at 45 mph, 45 ft and 90 ft; at 55 mph, 55 ft and 110 ft. Two tapers are different: the one-lane two-way taper in front of a flagger and the downstream taper use devices about 20 ft apart (Section 6B.08). How many cones for a taper: divide the taper length by the spacing and add one. A 245 ft taper at 35 mph takes 8 cones; a 540 ft taper at 45 mph takes 13. Warning lights on the devices, where used, follow the same spacing. Keep devices clean, upright and in line, and replace damaged ones (Standard). Tighter spacing is common at night, on curves and where drivers cut in. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6K.01 paras. 4-5, 14-15; Section 6B.08 paras. 12, 14

chunk.title: Cones, tubular markers and drums (barrels): how big and how tall
chunk.topic: Traffic control: cones, drums, barricades and arrow boards
chunk.text: Cones (Section 6K.03, Standard): mostly orange, made so a car can hit them without damage. At least 18 inches tall for daytime use on low-speed roads. At least 28 inches tall on freeways and other high-speed highways, at night on any road, and whenever more visible guidance is needed. For night use, a 28 to 36 inch cone has a 6 inch white reflective band 3 to 4 inches from the top and a 4 inch white band about 2 inches below it. Cones taller than 36 inches have alternating orange and white reflective stripes 4 to 6 inches wide, at least two of each, orange on top. Cones may be doubled up for weight. Tubular markers (Section 6K.04): at least 18 inches tall and 2 inches wide; 28 inches on freeways, high-speed roads and at night. Drums (Section 6K.06): at least 36 inches tall and 18 inches wide, lightweight and deformable, with orange and white reflective stripes 4 to 6 inches wide and a closed top; metal drums shall not be used and ballast shall not be put on top. All channelizing devices shall be crashworthy (Section 6K.01). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6K.01 para. 1, 6K.03 paras. 1-8, 6K.04 paras. 1-2, 6K.06 paras. 1-5

chunk.title: Barricades: Type 1, 2 and 3 and when each is used
chunk.topic: Traffic control: cones, drums, barricades and arrow boards
chunk.text: A barricade has one, two or three rails with orange and white reflective stripes sloping down at 45 degrees toward the side traffic is to pass. Type 1 has one rail, Type 2 two, Type 3 three. Stripes are 6 inches wide; 4 inch stripes may be used on rails shorter than 36 inches. Minimum rail length is 24 inches for Type 1 and Type 2 and 48 inches for Type 3, and each rail is 8 to 12 inches wide (Section 6K.07, Standard). Type 1 may be used on conventional roads and city streets where traffic keeps moving through the zone. Type 2 and Type 3 suit freeways, expressways and high-speed roads. Type 3 is the device for closing a road or part of one; it may run curb to curb. Sandbags for ballast go low on the frame, never on top rails where they can come through a windshield. Vertical panels (8 to 12 inches wide, at least 24 inches of striping) may be used where space is tight (Section 6K.05). Water-filled longitudinal channelizing devices are not crashworthy barrier: do not use them to shield the crew (Section 6K.10). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6K.05 paras. 1-4, 6K.07 paras. 3-22, 6K.10 paras. 1-8

chunk.title: Arrow boards: when the arrow is allowed and when it is caution only
chunk.topic: Traffic control: cones, drums, barricades and arrow boards
chunk.text: An arrow board in arrow or chevron mode is only for a stationary or moving lane closure on a multi-lane road (Section 6L.06, Standard). For shoulder work, for work beside the shoulder, for blocking the shoulder, and for closing one lane on a two-lane two-way road, the board shall be used only in caution mode (flashing caution or alternating diamond). An arrow board shows a lane closure, never a lane shift. Use one board for each closed lane. For a stationary closure it should sit on the shoulder at the start of the merging taper, or in the closed lane behind the cones if the shoulder is narrow. A vehicle carrying an arrow board shall also have high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating or strobe lights. Sizes (Figure 6L-3): Type A 48 by 24 inches for low-speed city streets; Type B 60 by 30 inches for intermediate speeds and for maintenance or mobile work on high-speed roads; Type C 96 by 48 inches for high-speed, high-volume roads. The board is dimmed at night, by at least half. An arrow board is required when a freeway lane is closed (TA-33). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6L.06 paras. 2-25; Figure 6L-3; Figure 6P-33 (TA-33) note 7

chunk.title: Night work: lighting, flagger stations and visibility
chunk.topic: Traffic control: night work
chunk.text: Night work has less traffic, but drivers see less, drive faster and are more often tired or impaired (Section 6A.05). What the MUTCD calls for: flagger stations shall be illuminated at night except in an emergency (Sections 6D.06, 6M.08 and 6N.18, Standard). Floodlights should light the work area, equipment crossings and other areas, set so they do not glare into the eyes of drivers, flaggers or workers; check by driving through from each direction after setup and again during the night. A driver should be able to tell a worker is a person, and shadows that hide workers should be kept down. Light levels the manual gives: about 5 foot-candles for general work, 10 foot-candles around equipment, 20 foot-candles for close, careful tasks. All signs and channelizing devices used at night are retroreflective or lit; cones are at least 28 inches with the two white bands. Flaggers at night should wear Class 3 apparel. Add lights and reflective markings to work vehicles and equipment. Where night traffic is light enough, closing the road and detouring traffic takes the traffic risk out of the work area. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6A.05, 6M.08 paras. 1-6, 6N.18 paras. 2-7, 6K.03, 6C.05 para. 7

chunk.title: Work duration: the five categories that decide how much traffic control
chunk.topic: Traffic control: short jobs and mobile work
chunk.text: The MUTCD sorts work by how long it occupies one spot (Section 6N.01, Standard). Long-term stationary: more than 3 days. Intermediate-term stationary: more than one daylight period up to 3 days, or night work lasting more than 1 hour. Short-term stationary: daytime work that occupies a location more than 1 hour within a single daylight period. Short duration: up to 1 hour. Mobile: work that moves intermittently or continuously. The manual notes that most maintenance and utility work is short-term stationary. Long-term and intermediate-term zones run into the night, so their devices shall be retroreflective or illuminated. Long-term jobs are where temporary barrier, drums and changed pavement markings make sense. For short-duration and mobile work, setting up and taking down a full layout can take longer than the work and expose the crew more, so simplified control is allowed, built around a work truck with high-intensity flashing lights; but safety should not be cut just because the location changes often. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6N.01 paras. 1-11

chunk.title: Short-duration (1 hour or less) and mobile work: what can be left out
chunk.topic: Traffic control: short jobs and mobile work
chunk.text: For work of 1 hour or less, and for mobile work, the MUTCD allows fewer devices if a vehicle with activated high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating or strobe lights is used. Work beyond the shoulder: for short-term, short-duration or mobile work all signs and cones may be left out (TA-1). Work on the shoulder: for 60 minutes or less the signs and cones may be left out (TA-3). Shoulder work with a small encroachment: for short-duration work the taper and cones may be left out if a shadow vehicle with lights is used (TA-6). In the center of an intersection: the cones may be left out for short-duration work if a vehicle with lights is in the work space (TA-26). Flaggers on a two-lane road: ROAD WORK AHEAD and END ROAD WORK may be left out for short-duration work, but the flagger signs stay (TA-10). Rules that do not bend (Standard): four-way hazard flashers may be added but shall not replace the high-intensity lights; an arrow board on a shoulder or two-lane road is in caution mode; signs on the truck are covered or turned when no work is going on. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6N.01 paras. 9-20; Figures 6P-1 note 4, 6P-3 note 5, 6P-6 note 10, 6P-10 note 3, 6P-26 note 6

chunk.title: Work off the road and on the shoulder: how much traffic control
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: Beyond the shoulder (Section 6N.05): work 15 ft or more from the edge of the traveled way generally needs no traffic control, unless trucks parked or entering, or equipment crossing, will distract drivers; then use a single ROAD WORK AHEAD sign, or SHOULDER WORK if vehicles are on the shoulder. The ROAD WORK AHEAD sign may be left out if the work is behind barrier, more than 24 inches behind the curb, or 15 ft or more from the road (TA-1). On the shoulder, road open (Section 6N.06): when a paved shoulder 8 ft or wider is closed, at least one advance warning sign shall be used, and channelizing devices shall close the shoulder ahead of the work, mark the start of the work space and keep traffic in the lanes (Standard). The shoulder taper is 1/3 L. An arrow board on the shoulder is in caution mode only. Shoulder work that takes part of a lane (Section 6N.07): unless the lane that is left is at least 10 ft wide, close the lane; 9 ft may be used for short-term work on low-volume, low-speed roads without wide trucks. This minor-encroachment setup is for low-speed minor roads; on faster roads close the lane (TA-6). The approved plan governs.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6N.05 paras. 1-4, 6N.06 paras. 2-9, 6N.07 paras. 2-4; Figures 6P-1 note 3, 6P-3 note 8, 6P-6 notes 1-4

chunk.title: Utility work in a street: the typical applications that fit
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: Section 6N.10 speaks to utility crews directly: utility work happens in and next to the road, often at intersections, with a small crew, few vehicles and few devices. To make up for fewer devices, use high-visibility ones, such as high-intensity flashing lights on the work trucks or a flag tree (Guidance). The manual names these typical applications as examples for utility work: TA-6 shoulder work with minor encroachment, TA-10 lane closure on a two-lane road using flaggers, TA-15 work in the center of a low-volume road, TA-18 lane closure on a minor street, TA-21 lane closure on the near side of an intersection, TA-22 and TA-23 lane closure on the far side of an intersection, TA-26 closure in the center of an intersection, and TA-33 stationary lane closure on a divided highway. Add TA-28 and TA-29 when a sidewalk or crosswalk is affected, and TA-1, TA-3 and TA-4 for work off the road or on the shoulder. A UTILITY WORK AHEAD sign (W21-7) may replace ROAD WORK AHEAD. In a street the plan also has to keep access to driveways and businesses, keep a bike route or sign another one, and keep access to any bus stop that is affected (Standard). The approved plan governs.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6N.10 paras. 2-10; Section 6H.24; Table 6P-1

chunk.title: Work at an intersection: near side, far side and in the middle
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: The MUTCD sorts intersection work by where the work space sits (Section 6N.12). Near side (before the intersection): handled like a mid-block lane closure (TA-21). The merging taper shall move traffic into the right lane or the left lane, not both; a left-hand taper keeps right-turning cars from blocking through traffic. Far side (past the intersection, TA-22 to TA-25): drivers arrive straight through and from both turns, so if a lane is closed on the far side, also close it on the near-side approach so nobody merges inside the intersection. In the middle (TA-26 and TA-27): keep the work space small so traffic can pass around it, with lanes at least 10 ft wide, or use flaggers or police to direct traffic, or stage the work, or close an approach. Put advance warning signs on every street that enters. If the work space crosses a crosswalk, close the crosswalk the way TA-29 shows. Think about the signal: detectors, timing and signal heads over a closed lane may need changes, and if you expect capacity, operation or pedestrian access problems you shall contact the agency that owns the signal (Standard). The approved plan governs.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6N.12 paras. 2-16; Figures 6P-21 notes 1-3, 6P-22 note 1, 6P-26 note 1, 6P-27 notes 1-2

chunk.title: Typical applications (TA drawings): how to use them
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: Chapter 6P of the MUTCD has 54 typical applications, TA-1 to TA-54, each a drawing (Figure 6P-1 to 6P-54) with a page of notes. Table 6P-1 is the index and Table 6P-2 explains the symbols. On the drawings the sign spacing is shown as letters A, B and C from Table 6B-1, and taper lengths come from the formulas in Table 6B-4. Most drawings show devices for one direction only. The typical applications are minimum solutions and are generally treated as Guidance; a note on the notes page that is labeled Standard is a requirement. A real plan often combines two or three of them, for example a near-side lane closure on one street, a far-side closure on the cross street and a crosswalk closure. The plan may add devices, lengthen sign spacing or tapers to give drivers more time, and adjust for the site, and devices marked optional may be left out. Positive protection (barrier or a truck-mounted attenuator) may be added to almost any of them. Your state DOT's standard plans or work zone manual usually replace these drawings on state roads. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6P.01 paras. 1-7; Tables 6P-1 and 6P-2; Section 6B.01 paras. 21-25

chunk.title: TA-10: lane closure on a two-lane road using flaggers
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: This is the standard setup when a trench takes one lane of a two-lane road. Advance signs in each direction: ROAD WORK AHEAD (or UTILITY WORK AHEAD), ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, then the Flagger sign, spaced A, B and C from Table 6B-1. A BE PREPARED TO STOP sign may be added between the Flagger sign and the ONE LANE ROAD sign. A flagger at each end, a short one-lane two-way taper of 50 to 100 ft in front of the work with cones about 20 ft apart, a buffer space if there is room, cones along the work at no more than 2 times the speed limit in feet, and a downstream taper. Notes: one flagger may be used on a short, low-volume, straight job where that flagger can be seen from both directions. ROAD WORK AHEAD and END ROAD WORK may be left out for short-duration work. Flagger stations shall be lit at night except in emergencies (Standard). On a curve or hill crest, lengthen the buffer so the taper and the back of the queue are seen in time. An automated flagger device may be used where only one lane approaches. An arrow board here is caution mode only. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Figure 6P-10 (TA-10) notes 1-13; Sections 6B.08, 6E.02, 6K.01, 6L.06 para. 18

chunk.title: TA-1, TA-3 and TA-4: work beyond the shoulder and on the shoulder
chunk.topic: Traffic control: typical setups for utility work
chunk.text: TA-1, work beyond the shoulder: one ROAD WORK AHEAD sign. The sign may be left out if the work space is behind a barrier, more than 24 inches behind the curb, or 15 ft or more from the edge of any roadway. For short-term, short-duration or mobile work, all signs and devices may be left out if a vehicle with activated high-intensity flashing lights is used. TA-3, work on the shoulder: SHOULDER WORK sign (a Workers sign may be used instead), a shoulder taper of 1/3 L and cones along the work. If a paved shoulder 8 ft or wider is closed, at least one advance warning sign and channelizing devices are required (Standard). For work of 60 minutes or less the signs and cones may be left out if a vehicle with activated lights is used. TA-4, short-duration or mobile work on a shoulder: stationary signs may be left out if the work vehicle shows high-intensity lights. In all three, four-way flashers do not replace the high-intensity lights, and an arrow board on the shoulder is caution mode only (Standard). Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Figures 6P-1 (TA-1) notes 2-6, 6P-3 (TA-3) notes 3-8, 6P-4 (TA-4) notes 1-9

chunk.title: TA-28 and TA-29: sidewalk detour and crosswalk closure
chunk.topic: Traffic control: pedestrians and sidewalks
chunk.text: TA-28, sidewalk detour or diversion (Standard notes): the temporary route shall be detectable and have accessibility features consistent with the existing sidewalk. A pedestrian channelizing device that a long cane can detect shall span the full width of the closed sidewalk. Temporary ramps shall be 12:1 (8.33 percent) or flatter with a slip-resistant surface, with a landing at least 48 by 48 inches and 2 percent cross-slope or flatter. SIDEWALK CLOSED CROSS HERE signs shall include an audible information device. The route may be 48 inches wide with a 60 inch passing area every 200 ft. TA-29, crosswalk closure and pedestrian detour: the temporary crossing has the same detectable and accessible rules; curb parking shall be prohibited for at least 50 ft ahead of a temporary mid-block crosswalk (Standard); pedestrian signal heads for a closed crosswalk should be covered or turned off. Both drawings show only the pedestrian devices; the lane closure signs for vehicles come from the other typical applications. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
chunk.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Figures 6P-28 (TA-28) notes 1-14, 6P-29 (TA-29) notes 1-11

chunk.title: OSHA rule for traffic control and flaggers: 1926.200(g) and 1926.201(a) follow the MUTCD
chunk.topic: Traffic control: OSHA rules
chunk.text: OSHA's construction rule on signs, signals and barricades is Subpart G. Two paragraphs make the MUTCD an OSHA requirement. 29 CFR 1926.200(g)(1): at points of hazard, construction areas shall be posted with legible traffic control signs and protected by traffic control devices. 1926.200(g)(2): the design and use of all traffic control devices, including signs, signals, markings, barricades and other devices, for the protection of construction workers shall conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD. 29 CFR 1926.201(a): signaling by flaggers and the use of flaggers, including their warning garments, shall conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD. So a missing taper, a flagger with no paddle or no vest, or a night flagger station with no light can be cited by OSHA as well as by the road agency. Subpart G today has only those two sections, 1926.200 and 1926.201; the old barricade section 1926.202 and definitions section 1926.203 are no longer in the rule (last amended at 84 FR 21577, May 14, 2019). Separately, 29 CFR 1926.651(d) requires high-visibility garments for excavation crews exposed to public traffic. States that run their own OSHA plan may have their own versions.
chunk.source: 29 CFR 1926.200(g)(1)-(2); 29 CFR 1926.201(a); 29 CFR part 1926 subpart G (sections list); 29 CFR 1926.651(d)
chunk.edition: 29 CFR part 1926 subpart G as amended at 84 FR 21577 (May 14, 2019)

chunk.title: Which MUTCD edition OSHA enforces
chunk.topic: Traffic control: OSHA rules
chunk.text: OSHA's construction rules name a specific edition of the MUTCD. 29 CFR 1926.6(n)(1) incorporates by reference the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices for Streets and Highways, 2009 Edition, December 2009, including Revision 1 dated May 2012 and Revision 2 dated May 2012, for 1926.200(g) and 1926.201(a). The Federal Highway Administration and the states have moved on to the 11th Edition (December 2023, with Revision 1 dated December 2025). In practice a setup that meets the current state manual and the approved traffic control plan is what the road agency requires, and the main Part 6 numbers a crew uses did not change between the two editions: the taper formulas, the 100, 350 and 500 ft sign spacings, the stopping sight distance table used for buffers and flagger stations, the 28 inch night cone, and Class 2 or 3 apparel. What changed is mostly the numbering (flaggers moved from Chapter 6E to 6D, typical applications from Chapter 6H to 6P) and newer provisions. If a citation or a contract quotes a section number, check which edition it is quoting.
chunk.source: 29 CFR 1926.6(n)(1); 29 CFR 1926.200(g)(2), 1926.201(a); MUTCD 11th Edition Part 6; OSHA highway work zones page (2009 Edition)
chunk.edition: 29 CFR 1926.6 as read 2026-11-20; MUTCD 2009 Edition with Revisions 1 and 2 (May 2012)
chunk.note: The statement that the main numbers did not change between editions rests on the 11th Edition tables read today and the 2009-based values already in the Ask KB (ords 1982-1988), not on a side-by-side read of the 2009 PDF.

chunk.text: Washington adopts the national MUTCD with state changes listed in chapter 468-95 WAC. WSDOT's page gives October 27, 2025 as the effective date for the 11th Edition in the state. Flaggers: every flagger must carry a valid state traffic control flagger card, with an expiration date no more than 3 years from issue, under WAC 296-155-305(6); the WSDOT Standard Specifications (1-10.3(1)A) say the same. Someone without a card may flag only in an emergency, until a certified flagger takes over. Cards from the reciprocity states are accepted: Oregon, Idaho and Montana. Tapers, sign spacing and cone spacing come from the national MUTCD Part 6 unless the state manual or the permit says otherwise: taper L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less and W x S at 45 mph or more. The approved traffic control plan governs.
chunk.source: WSDOT MUTCD page (11th Edition effective Oct. 27, 2025); chapter 468-95 WAC; WAC 296-155-305
chunk.edition: MUTCD 11th Edition with chapter 468-95 WAC modifications

chunk.title: West Virginia traffic control: which MUTCD applies and the flagger training rule
chunk.topic: Traffic control: which manual applies and flagger cards
chunk.text: West Virginia: an industry tracker lists the state as one that uses the national MUTCD with a state supplement, but its adoption of the 11th Edition was not confirmed from the state DOT's own page; ask the state DOT traffic office which edition is in force. Flaggers: Flaggers must be certified by passing ATSSA training. (WVDOH Standard Specifications Section 636.11.1.) This wording is the state document as posted by the national Work Zone Safety Information Clearinghouse on 2026-08-20; confirm it in the current spec book before you rely on it. Tapers, sign spacing and cone spacing come from the national MUTCD Part 6 unless the state manual or the permit says otherwise: taper L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less and W x S at 45 mph or more. The approved traffic control plan governs.
chunk.source: WVDOH Standard Specifications Section 636.11.1; adoption status not confirmed
chunk.edition: WVDOH Standard Specifications Section 636.11.1, as posted 2026-08-20

chunk.title: Wisconsin traffic control: which MUTCD applies and the flagger training rule
chunk.topic: Traffic control: which manual applies and flagger cards
chunk.text: Wisconsin: an industry tracker lists the state as one that has its own state MUTCD, but its adoption of the 11th Edition was not confirmed from the state DOT's own page; ask the state DOT traffic office which edition is in force. Wisconsin's manual is the WMUTCD. Flaggers: Since January 1, 2020 all flaggers on Wisconsin state highways must be certified (training meeting the Wisconsin Flagging Handbook). (WisDOT Standard Specifications Section 104.6.1.2.2.) This wording is the state document as posted by the national Work Zone Safety Information Clearinghouse on 2022-08-02; confirm it in the current spec book before you rely on it. Tapers, sign spacing and cone spacing come from the national MUTCD Part 6 unless the state manual or the permit says otherwise: taper L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less and W x S at 45 mph or more. The approved traffic control plan governs.

chunk.title: Wyoming traffic control: which MUTCD applies and the flagger training rule
chunk.topic: Traffic control: which manual applies and flagger cards
chunk.text: Wyoming: an industry tracker lists the state as one that uses the national MUTCD without a state manual of its own, but its adoption of the 11th Edition was not confirmed from the state DOT's own page; ask the state DOT traffic office which edition is in force. Flaggers: Complete and pass a training program approved by the State Construction Office before flagging (3-day grace in unplanned emergencies); current card on the project. How long it lasts: tested every 3 years. Accepted: Wyoming Flaggers Traffic Control Certification, ATSSA. (WYDOT Standard Specifications Section 703.4.6.) This wording is the state document as posted by the national Work Zone Safety Information Clearinghouse on 2024-08-05; confirm it in the current spec book before you rely on it. Tapers, sign spacing and cone spacing come from the national MUTCD Part 6 unless the state manual or the permit says otherwise: taper L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less and W x S at 45 mph or more. The approved traffic control plan governs.
chunk.source: WYDOT Standard Specifications Section 703.4.6; adoption status not confirmed
chunk.edition: WYDOT Standard Specifications Section 703.4.6, as posted 2024-08-05

chunk.title: California advance warning sign spacing by speed (CA MUTCD Table 6B-1)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: advance warning signs
chunk.text: California's Table 6B-1 in the CA MUTCD 2026 sets advance warning sign spacing by speed on urban streets, which the national table does not. Distances A, B and C are the same within each row. Urban, 25 mph or less: 100 ft. 30 mph: 150 ft. 35 mph: 200 ft. 40 mph: 250 ft. 45 mph: 300 ft. Urban, 50 mph or more: 350 ft. Rural: 500 ft. Expressway or freeway: A 1,000 ft, B 1,500 ft, C 2,640 ft. A is from the taper or point of restriction to the first sign, B from the first to the second sign, C from the second to the third. Use the posted speed limit, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed. So three signs on a 35 mph city street sit 200 ft apart, 600 ft in all. These are recommended minimums; the encroachment permit or the approved traffic control plan can ask for more, and on State highways the Caltrans Standard Plans govern.
chunk.source: CA MUTCD 2026 (Caltrans, eff. Jan. 18, 2026), Table 6B-1 and footnotes; Section 6B.04

chunk.title: California taper lengths by speed for a 12 ft lane (CA MUTCD Table 6B-3(CA))
chunk.topic: Traffic control: tapers and buffer spaces
chunk.text: California's CA MUTCD 2026 prints the taper lengths for a 12 ft offset in Table 6B-3(CA). Merging taper L, then shifting taper L/2, then shoulder taper L/3, in feet. 20 mph: 80, 40, 27. 25 mph: 125, 63, 42. 30 mph: 180, 90, 60. 35 mph: 245, 123, 82. 40 mph: 320, 160, 107. 45 mph: 540, 270, 180. 50 mph: 600, 300, 200. 55 mph: 660, 330, 220. 60 mph: 720, 360, 240. 65 mph: 780, 390, 260. 70 mph: 840, 420, 280. 75 mph: 900, 450, 300. Downstream taper: 50 ft, 100 ft maximum. For another width use the formula: W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less, W x S at 45 mph or more. S is the posted speed limit, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed. Devices in the downstream taper and in the one-lane two-way taper go about 20 ft apart. On State highways use the Caltrans Standard Plans for traffic control systems, T9 to T27 (Section 6B.08).
chunk.source: CA MUTCD 2026, Section 6B.08 paras. 4, 8, 12, 14, 16; Tables 6B-3, 6B-3(CA), 6B-4

chunk.title: California flagger training rule and paddle (CA MUTCD 6D.01, 8 CCR 1599)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: California does not issue a state flagger card, but training is mandatory. The CA MUTCD 2026 adds a California Standard to Section 6D.01: flaggers shall be trained in the proper fundamentals of flagging moving traffic before being assigned as flaggers. The training covers nine topics, among them flagger equipment, the layout of the work zone, signaling to stop, proceed and slow, one-way traffic control, emergency vehicles, handling emergencies, hostile drivers, and flagging alone. The trainer shall have the qualifications and experience to teach it, and the employer shall keep the training records required by its Injury and Illness Prevention Program (8 CCR 3203). The Cal/OSHA rule is Construction Safety Orders section 1599. Paddle: a 24 by 24 inch STOP/SLOW paddle may be used where more emphasis is needed and speeds are 30 mph or more; on a staff, the bottom of the paddle should be at least 6 ft above the pavement. Flags are for emergencies, at least 24 inches square. Apparel is ANSI/ISEA 107-2015 Class 2 or 3, Class 3 recommended for flaggers at night (Section 6C.05). Flagger stations shall be lit at night except in emergencies.
chunk.source: CA MUTCD 2026, Sections 6D.01 paras. 2-5, 6D.02 paras. 4, 5a, 6D.03, 6D.06 para. 5, 6C.05; 8 CCR 1599, 3203

chunk.title: California work zone fines and construction speed zones (CVC 42009, 22362)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: California Vehicle Code 42009 raises the penalty for listed moving violations in a highway construction or maintenance area: a misdemeanor fine is doubled, and an infraction is charged one category higher on the uniform traffic penalty schedule. It applies only when workers are actually doing the work and traffic control devices or warning signs tell drivers the workers are there. The listed offenses include speeding, obeying traffic devices, passing, right-of-way, turning, reckless driving and DUI. Speed zones: the CA MUTCD 2026 (Section 6B.01) says a reduced construction speed limit under Vehicle Code 22362 has to be documented in writing, cannot be set below 25 mph, is posted only where the work affects traffic, and the signs are covered or removed in non-working hours unless the condition is still there. Vehicle Code 21367 lets the agency doing the work regulate traffic through it. The contractor cannot post a regulatory speed limit on its own; the agency orders it.
chunk.source: Cal. Veh. Code 42009(a)-(c); Veh. Code 22362, 21367; CA MUTCD 2026 Section 6B.01 paras. 19a, 20c-20p
chunk.edition: Cal. Veh. Code 42009 as read 2026-11-20; CA MUTCD 2026
chunk.note: Vehicle Code text read on a third-party mirror (california.public.law); confirm on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

chunk.title: Arizona work zone double fines (A.R.S. 28-710) and the signs
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Arizona doubles the cost of speeding in a state highway work zone when workers are present. A.R.S. 28-710: in a state highway work zone marked by traffic control devices that show where it begins and ends, a driver may not exceed the speed shown on the devices; if workers are present, the driver pays the normal civil penalty plus an additional assessment equal to it. Half of the extra goes to the state highway work zone safety fund and half to the state highway fund. Signs: the Arizona Supplement to the MUTCD (Section 6G.08) says double fine signs in state highway work zones go up only when workers are present and come down or are covered when they are not, existing speed limit signs inside the double fine area are covered, and the layout should follow the ADOT Temporary Traffic Control Design Guidelines. Leaving the double fine signs up with no crew there is not allowed under that section. City streets are not state highway work zones under this statute.
chunk.source: A.R.S. 28-710(A)-(D); A.R.S. 28-652; ADOT Arizona Supplement to the MUTCD 11th Edition (Jan. 2026) Section 6G.08

chunk.title: Nevada double penalties in work zones (NRS 484B.130)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Nevada adds a second penalty, equal to the first, for speeding and other listed traffic offenses in a temporary traffic control zone (NRS 484B.130). It applies when construction, maintenance or repair workers are present, or when the road condition, such as narrowed or shifted lanes or an uneven surface, makes the violation more dangerous. The added penalty is capped at $1,000, 6 months in jail or 120 hours of community service. Signs are part of it: the agency or its contractor must put up a sign before the zone reading DOUBLE PENALTIES IN WORK ZONES, a sign at the beginning of the zone and a sign at the end. If the signs are missing the double penalty generally does not apply, unless the violation injured a worker or did $1,000 or more in property damage. Signs are not required for emergency zones or on roads posted 25 mph or less next to residential areas, and there the double penalty applies only with a worker injury or $1,000 or more in damage. So on a Nevada job, the three signs are the contractor's to set.
chunk.note: Read on nevada.public.law (mirror, accessed text dated May 2025); confirm on leg.state.nv.us.

chunk.title: Texas work zone fines double when workers are present (Transp. Code 472.022)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Texas Transportation Code 472.022 makes it an offense to disobey a warning sign or drive around a barricade, with a fine of $1 to $200. If it happens in a construction or maintenance work zone while workers are present, and the citation says so, the fine is $2 to $400. A stretch of road only counts as a construction or maintenance work zone for this purpose if it is marked by signs that say it is a work zone, show where the zone begins and ends, and state: Fines double when workers present. Mobile operations, as the Texas MUTCD defines them, are not included. Driving around a barricade placed because water is over the road is a Class B misdemeanor. For a crew this means the begin, end and fines-double signs have to be in the setup for the higher fines to apply.
chunk.source: Tex. Transp. Code 472.022
chunk.edition: Tex. Transp. Code 472.022, current as of Jan. 1, 2026
chunk.note: Read on FindLaw (current as of 2026-01-01); confirm on statutes.capitol.texas.gov.

chunk.title: Florida speeding fines double in a posted construction zone (s. 318.18(3)(e))
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Florida doubles the speeding fine in a posted construction zone under section 318.18(3)(e), Florida Statutes. Two conditions: the zone is posted, with the posting stating the speed limit and that fines are doubled; and construction personnel are present or operating equipment on the road or immediately next to it. The regular fines in 318.18(3)(b) are $25 for 6 to 9 mph over, $100 for 10 to 14 over, $150 for 15 to 19 over, $175 for 20 to 29 over and $250 for 30 mph or more over, so doubled they are $50, $200, $300, $350 and $500, before court costs. No crew on or beside the road means no doubling, even with the signs up. FDOT work zone layouts are in the FDOT Standard Plans, Index 102 series, and FDOT requires its Temporary Traffic Control (MOT) training for people who set up and supervise work zones on state roads; those two points were not confirmed from an FDOT page here.

chunk.title: Washington flagger card rule (WAC 296-155-305)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
chunk.text: Washington requires a flagger card by state safety rule. WAC 296-155-305(6): each flagger must have in their possession a valid Washington traffic control flagger card, or a valid card from a state that has a reciprocity agreement with Washington. The card shows the training completed, the date, the instructor, the issuing state and an expiration date no more than 3 years from issue, with a photo or the words valid with photo ID. Training is based on the MUTCD. The reciprocity states named are Oregon, Idaho and Montana, and the WSDOT standard specifications (1-10.3(1)A) likewise accept cards from those states. Someone without a card may flag only in an emergency, until a certified flagger takes over. Other points in the same rule: flaggers are used only when other traffic control is not enough; the employer orients each flagger to the site (the job, equipment, traffic pattern, signals with operators, an escape route on foot); a site-specific traffic control plan is kept on site for jobs longer than one day; flaggers may not be given other duties or use a cell phone or headphones while flagging; and they get a paid 10 minute rest for each 4 hours.
chunk.source: WAC 296-155-305(2), (6), (7), (9); WSDOT Standard Specifications 1-10.3(1)A

chunk.title: Washington speeding in a roadway construction zone: double penalty (RCW 46.61.527)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Washington doubles the penalty for speeding in a roadway construction zone. RCW 46.61.527: a roadway construction zone is an area where public employees or private contractors are doing construction, repair or maintenance work on or next to a public road. A driver may not exceed the speed shown on the traffic control devices in the zone, and a speed infraction there carries twice the usual penalty, which may not be waived, reduced or suspended. The same section creates the crime of reckless endangerment of roadway workers, a gross misdemeanor: driving in a construction zone in a way that endangers or is likely to endanger people or property, or removing, evading or intentionally striking a traffic safety or control device. A conviction brings a 60 day license suspension. Standards for the devices on state highways are set by the Secretary of Transportation. The text read here showed amendments through 2009; later changes were not confirmed.

chunk.title: Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook (OTTCH): the rules for jobs of 3 days or less
chunk.topic: Traffic control: which manual applies and flagger cards
chunk.text: Oregon's standard for short work zones is the Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook, 2026 edition (January 2026), adopted through OAR 734-020-0005. It covers traffic control in place continuously for three days or less on any public road in the state. Longer jobs, or jobs more complicated than the handbook's diagrams, need a full traffic control plan. A traffic control plan is required whenever work is done on or along a public road; for short jobs the handbook diagram can be the plan. Flaggers: certified in Oregon, Washington, Idaho or Montana, at least 18 years old, retrained every three years, carrying the card (sections 3.2 and 3.3). When only flaggers are used, the distance between the Flagger signs should not be more than one mile; past that use a pilot car. Drivers should not be held longer than 20 minutes at a flagger station under normal conditions. Apparel: ANSI/ISEA 107-2015 or later, Type R, Class 2 or 3; flaggers Class 2 required and Class 3 recommended at night. Cone spacing: the posted speed in feet in a taper and twice that along the work. Cities and counties may be stricter and usually require a permit.
chunk.source: Oregon Temporary Traffic Control Handbook 2026 (ODOT), sections 1.1, 1.4, 2.3, 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 3.8; OAR 734-020-0005

chunk.title: Colorado work zone penalties and the signs that turn them on (C.R.S. 42-4-614)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Colorado increases penalties and surcharges for listed traffic violations inside a designated maintenance, repair or construction zone (C.R.S. 42-4-614, with the amounts in 42-4-1701(4)(c)). CDOT designates the zone on a state highway; on any other road the public entity doing the work does. A zone can be designated only when work is going on or will be within four hours. Signs make the zone: one sign before the work area telling drivers that increased penalties are in effect, and one after it telling them the increased penalties no longer apply. The zone runs from the first sign to the second. The signs must meet CDOT's requirements and may be on fixed, variable or movable stands, or on a moving vehicle for work such as striping. The size of the increase was not confirmed here; it is set in section 42-4-1701. Colorado flagger notes from CDOT: flaggers must speak and understand English, and fluorescent red apparel is not allowed for flaggers.
chunk.source: C.R.S. 42-4-614; C.R.S. 42-4-1701(4)(c); CDOT Flagger Program industry memo (Jan. 1, 2026)

chunk.title: Utah: obey the flagger, and double fines for speeding past workers (41-6a-209)
chunk.topic: Traffic control: work zone speed and fines
chunk.text: Utah Code 41-6a-209 does two things. First, it is an offense to willfully fail or refuse to obey a lawful order or direction of a flagger at a highway construction or maintenance site who is using the devices and procedures required, the same as disobeying a peace officer or a school crossing guard. Second, for speeding in a highway construction or maintenance site, the court must set the fine at no less than double the amount in the uniform recommended fine schedule, but only if workers are present at the site and the site is clearly marked with signs warning drivers of the doubled fine. Without workers there, or without the signs, the doubling does not apply. Flaggers in the state must be trained and certified before flagging, and the certification lasts three years (UDOT Flagger Training and Certification page). The section's last listed amendment is from the 2005 General Session; later changes were not confirmed.
chunk.source: Utah Code 41-6a-209; UDOT Flagger Training & Certification page

chunk.title: Washington WSDOT storm sewer tests (Section 7-04)
chunk.topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
chunk.text: Washington (WSDOT M 41-10, 2027 edition, Section 7-04.3(1), storm sewers). Exfiltration test: leakage no more than 1 gallon per hour per inch of diameter per 100 feet, with at least 6 feet of water above the crown; the allowance rises 10 percent for each extra 2 feet of head, and pressure at the low-end invert is capped at 16 feet of water (7-04.3(1)B). Infiltration test: no more than 0.8 gallon per hour per inch of diameter per 100 feet (7-04.3(1)C). Low-pressure air test: the pressure-drop time must be at least the table time, for example 80 seconds for 100 feet of 12-inch pipe; pipe that does not pass air (plastic, lined) needs four times the table time; pipe over 30 inches is tested joint by joint under ASTM C1103 (7-04.3(1)E and F). Sanitary sewers are stricter: see Section 7-17.
chunk.source: WSDOT Standard Specifications for Road, Bridge, and Municipal Construction, M 41-10, 2027 edition, Division 7 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Washington WSDOT manholes, catch basins, side sewers and cleanouts (Sections 7-05, 7-18, 7-19)
chunk.topic: Spec books: manholes, inlets and catch basins
chunk.text: Washington (WSDOT M 41-10, 2027 edition). Manholes, inlets and catch basins (7-05): dig to leave 1 foot clear between the structure and the bank; ladder rungs at 12 inches; rigid pipe entering a sanitary manhole needs a flexible joint within 1.5 pipe diameters or 18 inches of the wall, whichever is greater; manholes over 10 feet are paid per extra foot; an abandoned manhole is broken down to at least 4 feet below the new surface and filled with sand compacted to 90 percent. Side sewers (7-18): joint deflection never more than 2 inches per foot, use 1/8 bends for bigger turns; a 6-inch test tee goes where the side sewer crosses the right-of-way line; mark the end with a 2x4 stake 4 feet long buried 3 feet. Cleanouts (7-19): at each total 90 degrees of change in grade or alignment, never more than 100 feet apart, same size as the side sewer.
chunk.source: WSDOT Standard Specifications for Road, Bridge, and Municipal Construction, M 41-10, 2027 edition, Division 7 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas TxDOT pipe excavation, bedding and backfill (Items 400, 401, 402)
chunk.topic: Spec books: trench, bedding, backfill and compaction
chunk.text: Texas (TxDOT 2024 Standard Specifications). Item 400, Excavation and Backfill for Structures: pipe gets Class C bedding unless the plans show something else; for precast concrete pipe the ASTM C1479 beddings are allowed (400.3.2). Pipe backfill goes in uniform layers no more than 8 inches deep (loose), each lift compacted mechanically, with the haunches thoroughly compacted (400.3.3.3); each layer must meet the density required for the roadbed (400.3.3.1; the percent comes from the embankment item and the plans, not Item 400). Cement-stabilized backfill: at least 7 percent cement by dry weight of aggregate, placed and compacted within 2 hours of mixing (400.3.3.4). Flowable backfill (Item 401, Table 2): excavatable mix 80 to 200 psi at 28 days; non-excavatable over 200 psi. Trench protection (Item 402): furnish and place excavation protection for trenches 5 feet or greater in depth, following OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P.
chunk.source: TxDOT Standard Specifications for Construction and Maintenance of Highways, Streets, and Bridges, 2024, Items 400, 401, 402 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas TxDOT concrete pipe, metal pipe, box culverts; fill before equipment crosses new pipe (Items 460, 462, 464)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Texas (TxDOT 2024 Standard Specifications). Item 464, Reinforced Concrete Pipe: circular pipe Classes I through V (D-loads 800 to 3,000); joints may be mortar, cold-applied asphalt joint compound, rubber gaskets (ASTM C1619 Class A or C) or preformed flexible sealant (ASTM C990); arch and elliptical pipe need at least 1 foot of cover; do not run heavy earth-moving equipment over the pipe until at least 4 feet of compacted fill is in place unless the plans or the Engineer allow it in writing (464.3.1). Item 460, Corrugated Metal Pipe: lay from the outlet end with laps pointing upstream; same 4-foot rule for heavy earth-moving equipment (460.3.2); bell-and-spigot gaskets to ASTM F477 with at least a 6-inch stab depth. Item 462, Concrete Box Culverts: no more than four lifting holes per precast section, each 3 inches or smaller; boxes with joints that are not mortar can be backfilled right away. Jacking, boring or tunneling any of these is under Item 476.
chunk.source: TxDOT Standard Specifications, 2024, Items 460, 462, 464 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas TxDOT thermoplastic pipe (HDPE, PP, PVC): backfill, mandrel and deflection limits (Item 468)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Texas (TxDOT 2024 Standard Specifications, Item 468, Thermoplastic Pipe). Bedding at least 4 inches thick, 6 inches where large rocks are present (468.3). Granular backfill goes in uniform loose layers about 6 inches deep up to 12 inches above the pipe; within 12 inches of the pipe use only hand-operated tampers; with flowable backfill the trench is pipe outside diameter plus 12 inches, the fill is carried at least 12 inches above the pipe, and you wait 24 hours before backfilling the rest (468.3.11). Stop backfilling if measured deflection passes 5 percent. No heavy earth-moving equipment over the pipe until at least 4 feet of compacted fill is in place (468.3.12). Final inspection (468.4.1): at least 30 days after backfill is complete, pull a mandrel sized at 95 percent of the pipe diameter through the whole length; if it will not pass, a 92.5 percent mandrel is tried and a remote camera is used to look at joints, cracks, deflection and ponding. Pipe deflected more than 7.5 percent of nominal diameter must be fixed or replaced (468.4.2). Joints: the bell must overlap at least two corrugations of the spigot.
chunk.source: TxDOT Standard Specifications, 2024, Item 468 Thermoplastic Pipe (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas TxDOT jacking, boring and tunneling pipe; manholes and inlets (Items 476, 465, 479)
chunk.topic: Spec books: jacking, boring and tunneling
chunk.text: Texas (TxDOT 2024 Standard Specifications). Item 476, Jacking, Boring, or Tunneling Pipe or Box: line and grade may not vary more than 1 inch in 10 feet; over-excavation no more than 2 inches at the top and sides, and anything over 1 inch is pressure grouted; do not excavate more than 2 feet ahead of the pipe; keep jacking going without interruption so the pipe does not set up; parallel jacked or tunneled lines need at least 3 feet clear between them; use plywood cushions between pipe ends, 1/2 inch minimum for pipe 30 inches and smaller and 3/4 inch for larger pipe and boxes; boring starts with a 2-inch pilot hole; keep a 3:1 slope from the edge of pavement on the shaft side. Item 465, Junction Boxes, Manholes, and Inlets: structures with rubber boots, gaskets or preformed sealant joints can be backfilled right away; place and compact backfill so the structure does not move. Item 479, adjusting manholes and inlets: flexible extension rings no taller than 3 inches; when capping, remove the structure to at least 1 foot below subgrade. Item 471 castings are load tested at 40,000 lb on a 9 by 9 inch block for 1 minute.
chunk.source: TxDOT Standard Specifications, 2024, Items 465, 471, 476, 479 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: California Caltrans structure backfill and compaction numbers (Sections 19-3, 19-5)
chunk.topic: Spec books: trench, bedding, backfill and compaction
chunk.text: California (Caltrans 2025 Standard Specifications, Section 19 Earthwork). Structure backfill, which is what goes around culverts and drainage structures: layers no more than 0.67 foot (8 inches) thick before compacting; relative compaction at least 95 percent; at least 90 percent is allowed at overside drains, headwalls, endwalls, culvert wingwalls and similar spots with nothing under pavement (19-3.03E(1)). Ponding and jetting is allowed only where the backfill drains freely and the foundation will not soften, in layers up to 4 feet, never in the top 4 feet below finished grade, and with vibratory compaction added.
