Slurry cement backfill: at least 188 lb of cement per cubic yard, placed within 1 hour of mixing, and nothing placed over it for at least 4 hours (19-3.02E, 19-3.03F). Soil cement bedding: at least 282 lb of cement per cubic yard and an 8-hour wait (19-3.02F(3), 19-3.03H). Embankment (19-5): 95 percent for 0.5 foot below the grading plane and 2.5 feet below finished grade under the traveled way plus 3 feet each side; 90 percent elsewhere. Caltrans 'relative compaction' is by California Test 216/231, not Proctor.
chunk.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications, 2025, Sections 19-3 and 19-5 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: California Caltrans drainage pipe joints and leak tests (Section 61)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: California (Caltrans 2025 Standard Specifications, Section 61, Drainage Facilities, general). Pipe materials have their own sections: plastic pipe Section 64, concrete pipe Section 65, corrugated metal pipe Section 66. Watertight joints are proven by holding a 10-foot head of water above the pipe crown for 10 minutes (61-2.01D(2)(b)). Field leak testing is done on culverts and drainage structures only where the plans show it (61-2.01D(3)(a)); the low-pressure air test is not used on drainage pipe over 30 inches (61-2.01D(3)(c)). Concrete backfill in pipe trenches is consolidated with high-frequency internal vibrators, and with rapid-strength concrete nothing goes on top until it reaches 500 psi (61-5.03). For plastic pipe in saturated clay, unsuitable material is removed at least 1/4 of the pipe diameter, and not less than 6 inches, each side of the pipe. Not confirmed here: Caltrans minimum cover for construction loads and plastic pipe deflection limits (Sections 64 to 66); read the section or the plans.
chunk.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications, 2025, Section 61 Drainage Facilities (read 2026-11-20; sections 64-66 not read)

chunk.title: Colorado CDOT structure backfill and compaction (Section 206)
chunk.topic: Spec books: trench, bedding, backfill and compaction
chunk.text: Colorado (CDOT 2025 Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, Section 206, Structure Excavation and Backfill). Structure backfill is Class 1 or Class 2, or Flow-Fill. Each layer of backfill is 6 inches or less. Both classes are compacted to at least 95 percent of maximum dry density, within plus or minus 2 percent of optimum moisture (soils with more than 35 percent passing the No. 200 sieve at 0 to 3 percent above optimum). Maximum density is by AASHTO T 180 for Class 1 and for A-1, A-2-4, A-2-5 and A-3 soils, and by AASHTO T 99 (as modified by CP 23) for other Class 2 materials (206.03). Flow-Fill is not compacted and goes in lifts of 3 feet or less unless the Engineer approves more; the next lift waits until the surface dents less than 3 inches with no visible water (ASTM D6024). Do not backfill against new concrete until it reaches 0.8 f'c. Bed course material is per 703.07 (206.02(b)).
chunk.source: CDOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, 2025, Section 206 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Colorado CDOT culverts and sewers: bedding, joints, 5 percent deflection, leak test (Sections 603, 604)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Colorado (CDOT 2025 Standard Specifications, Section 603, Culverts and Sewers). Bedding: a layer of loose structure backfill at least 3 inches thick (603.05). In new embankment, build the fill to at least 0.3 times the pipe outside diameter or rise before trenching for the pipe. Storm drain joints must be watertight; sanitary sewer concrete pipe uses rubber gaskets (603.07). Deflection of metal and plastic pipe: 5 percent maximum, measured 30 days or more after installation with a mandrel, laser profile or another approved method; replaced pipe is retested after another 30 days (603.10). Reinforced concrete pipe gets a visual inspection per AASHTO LRFD Section 27.6. Sanitary sewer leak limit: no more than 0.6 gallon per inch of inside diameter per 100 feet per hour (603.09). Jacked pipe: no trenching; grout the outside with 1 part portland cement to 3 parts fine aggregate. Section 604, manholes and inlets: a manhole in pavement is not built to final grade until the paving is done; pay depth is in 5-foot steps (0 to 5.0 ft pays as 5, 5.1 to 10.0 as 10).
chunk.source: CDOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, 2025, Sections 603 and 604 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Ten States Standards for sewers: manhole spacing, drops, alignment, steep slopes (Chapter 30)
chunk.topic: Sewer design standards: slopes, manholes, sizes
chunk.text: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014 edition, Chapter 30, Design of Sewers). Many state environmental agencies review sewer plans against this book or their own version of it. Manhole spacing (34.1): no more than 400 feet for sewers 15 inches and smaller, 500 feet for 18 to 30 inches, and up to 600 feet where modern cleaning equipment is available. Drop manhole (34.2): a drop pipe is needed when the incoming sewer is 24 inches or more above the manhole invert; under 24 inches the invert is filleted. Manhole size (34.3): at least 48 inches in diameter with a 24-inch minimum access opening. Alignment (33.5): sewers 24 inches and smaller are laid straight between manholes and checked by laser or lamping. Slope must be uniform between manholes (33.44). Velocities over 10 feet per second need protection against scour (33.45). Sewers on slopes of 20 percent or more are anchored: every 36 feet on 20 to 35 percent grades, 24 feet on 35 to 50 percent, 16 feet at 50 percent and steeper (33.46). Your state's own design rule and the project specs govern.
chunk.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), GLUMRB, 2014 edition, Chapter 30 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Ten States Standards sewer tests: 100 gallon leakage limit, air test standards, 5 percent deflection, manhole test
chunk.topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
chunk.text: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014 edition). Leakage tests (33.9): by water, leakage in or out must not exceed 100 gallons per inch of pipe diameter per mile per day, tested with at least 2 feet of positive head (33.94); by air, follow ASTM C828 for clay pipe, ASTM C924 for concrete pipe and ASTM F1417 for plastic pipe (33.95). Deflection test (33.85): required for all flexible pipe, run after the final backfill has been in place at least 30 days; no pipe may exceed 5 percent deflection; the rigid ball or mandrel is at least 95 percent of the pipe's base or average inside diameter and is pulled by hand, with no mechanical pulling devices. Manholes (34.7): inspected and tested for watertightness before going into service; air (vacuum) testing of concrete manholes follows ASTM C1244. Project specs are often tighter than these numbers, so read the testing section of your contract.
chunk.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), GLUMRB, 2014 edition, Chapter 30 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Ten States Standards: sewer and water main separation, 10 feet and 18 inches (Section 38)
chunk.topic: Water and sewer separation distances
chunk.text: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014 edition, Section 38, protection of water supplies). Side by side (38.31): sewers are laid at least 10 feet horizontally from any existing or proposed water main, measured edge to edge. Where 10 feet is not practical the reviewing agency can allow closer on a case-by-case basis if the water main is in a separate trench, or on an undisturbed earth shelf at one side of the sewer trench, with the bottom of the water main at least 18 inches above the top of the sewer. If neither can be done, both lines are built of slip-on or mechanical joint pipe rated at least 150 psi and pressure tested. Crossings (38.32): at least 18 inches between the outside of the water main and the outside of the sewer, whether the water main is above or below; keep sewer joints as far as possible from water main joints. If 18 inches cannot be met, either build the sewer to water pipe standards and pressure test it, or encase the water main or the sewer in a watertight carrier pipe that extends 10 feet on both sides of the crossing. State rules vary: check the state's own separation rule.
chunk.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), GLUMRB, 2014 edition, Chapter 30 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Montana water main rules: pressure, hydrants, sewer separation (Circular DEQ-1, Chapter 8)
chunk.topic: Spec books: water main installation, pressure test and disinfection
chunk.text: Montana (DEQ Circular DEQ-1, Standards for Water Works, 2022 edition, Chapter 8). Pressure (8.2.1): at least 35 psi normal working pressure and at least 20 psi under all flow conditions; normal working pressure should be about 60 to 80 psi. Size (8.2.2): mains serving fire hydrants are at least 6 inches; at least 3 inches where there is no fire protection. Hydrants (8.4): 6-inch lead; hydrant drains may not connect to, or be within 10 feet of, sanitary sewers or storm drains. Installation (8.7): continuous uniform bedding; enough cover to prevent freezing; pressure and leakage tests per the AWWA standards; flushing, disinfection and bacteria testing per AWWA C651. Separation from sewers (8.8): at least 10 feet horizontal, edge to edge, from gravity sanitary or storm sewers (8.8.2); at least 18 inches vertical at crossings, outside to outside (8.8.3), with reduced crossings down to 6 inches only under listed conditions such as a 150 psi tested sewer and encasement or flowable fill 10 feet each side; force mains 10 feet horizontal and 18 inches vertical (8.8.4); no water pipe through or touching a sewer manhole, and mains should be at least 10 feet from manholes (8.8.5).
chunk.source: Montana DEQ Circular DEQ-1, Standards for Water Works, 2022 edition, Chapter 8 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Ductile iron pipe joints: mechanical joint bolt torque and maximum joint deflection (DIPRA guide)
chunk.topic: Pipe installation guides by material
chunk.text: Ductile iron pipe joints, summarized from the DIPRA Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe (revised May 2015). Mechanical joint bolt torque (Table 4): 5/8 inch bolts on 3 inch joints 45 to 60 ft-lb; 3/4 inch bolts on 4 to 24 inch 75 to 90 ft-lb; 1 inch bolts on 30 to 36 inch 100 to 120 ft-lb; 1-1/4 inch bolts on 42 to 48 inch 120 to 150 ft-lb. Tighten in a star pattern and go around again until every bolt is in range. Push-on joints: clean the bell groove and the spigot, seat the gasket, lubricate the gasket and the plain end (not the socket), bevel field cuts, push straight home and deflect only after the joint is made. Maximum push-on deflection on an 18-foot length (Table 5): 5 degrees, about 19 inches of offset, for 3 to 12 inch; 3 degrees, about 11 inches, for 14 to 42 inch. Mechanical joints (Table 6): 6 inch 7 degrees (27 inches); 8 to 12 inch 5 degrees (20 inches); 14 inch 3.5 degrees; 24 inch about 2 degrees. Cutting: abrasive saw (about a minute per inch of diameter), then grind and bevel the end. Check the pipe maker's own table for the exact joint: restrained joints allow less.
chunk.source: Ductile Iron Pipe Research Association (DIPRA), Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, revised May 2015, hosted by McWane (our summary; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Water main pressure test, flushing and chlorination basics (DIPRA guide, AWWA C600 and C651)
chunk.topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
chunk.text: Testing a new ductile iron water main, summarized from the DIPRA Installation Guide (revised May 2015), which follows AWWA C600 and C651. Pressure test: at least 1.5 times the working pressure at the lowest point of the section, held for at least 2 hours (150 psi working means a 225 psi test). Measure the make-up water needed to hold pressure; examples of the testing allowance at 150 psi are about 0.50 gallon per hour per 1,000 feet of 6 inch and 0.99 for 12 inch. Brace or restrain temporary plugs and caps. Flush at 3.0 feet per second: roughly 400 gpm for a 6 inch main and 1,060 gpm for a 12 inch. Chlorination (AWWA C651): tablet method, granules at the start and every 500 feet and 5-gram tablets at joints, fill slowly at 1 foot per second or less, hold 24 hours (48 hours if the water is colder than 41 F), about 25 mg/L; continuous feed, at least 25 mg/L going in and at least 10 mg/L left after 24 hours; slug method, at least 100 mg/L for at least 3 hours, start over if it drops below 50 mg/L. Flush the strong chlorine out within about a day, dechlorinate where the discharge rule requires it, then take bacteria samples. The water agency's spec governs.
chunk.source: Ductile Iron Pipe Research Association (DIPRA), Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, revised May 2015, hosted by McWane (our summary; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Thrust blocks at bends and dead ends: forces, soil bearing values, how strong the concrete (DIPRA guide)
chunk.topic: Thrust blocks and restrained joints
chunk.text: Thrust restraint basics, summarized from the DIPRA Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe (revised May 2015). Water pressure pushes on every bend, tee, reducer, valve and dead end. Example thrust at 100 psi: a 12 inch 90 degree bend pushes about 19,353 lb and a 12 inch dead end about 13,685 lb; thrust scales straight with pressure, so use test pressure, not working pressure. Example soil bearing values at 4 feet deep (Table 8): muck 0, sand about 4,000 lb per square foot, hard clay about 9,000. Common practice is block bearing area = thrust divided by the allowable soil bearing, poured against undisturbed soil. Blocks are concrete of at least 2,000 psi, cured at least five days before testing. Mechanical joints by themselves hold no thrust. Restrained joints (or wedge-action glands) are used instead of blocks where space is tight or the soil behind the block may be dug out later; the restrained length comes from the engineer or the agency table. Always build what the plans or the agency thrust block detail shows; these numbers are examples, not a design.
chunk.source: Ductile Iron Pipe Research Association (DIPRA), Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, revised May 2015, hosted by McWane (our summary; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: ADS N-12 corrugated HDPE pipe: minimum and maximum cover (TN 2.01)
chunk.topic: Pipe cover: minimum and maximum burial depth
chunk.text: Corrugated HDPE storm pipe cover, summarized from ADS Technical Note TN 2.01 (rev. AB, 2024) for N-12 pipe. Minimum cover under H-20, H-25 or HL-93 traffic: 1 foot over the crown for 4 to 48 inch pipe and 2 feet for 54 and 60 inch; flexible pavement thickness does not count toward it, and construction or paving equipment may need more temporary cover (see the ADS Drainage Handbook installation section). Maximum cover depends on the backfill around the pipe. Examples in feet for 12 / 24 / 36 / 48 / 60 inch: Class 1 compacted stone 35 / 28 / 26 / 25 / 25; Class 2 at 95 percent 24 / 20 / 18 / 17 / 17; Class 2 at 90 percent 17 / 13 / 12 / 11 / 11; Class 2 at 85 percent 8 / 7 / 7 / 7 / 6; Class 3 at 95 percent 17 / 14 / 13 / 12 / 12; Class 3 at 90 percent 11 / 10 / 9 / 7 / 7. The table assumes installation per ASTM D2321, no groundwater pressure and 120 pcf soil. These are general guidance, not a project design, and other makers' pipe has its own tables.
chunk.source: ADS (Advanced Drainage Systems) Technical Note TN 2.01, Minimum and Maximum Burial Depth for Corrugated HDPE Pipe (per AASHTO), rev. AB, copyright 2024 (our summary; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Concrete pipe acceptance tests: infiltration, exfiltration, air, joint and vacuum tests (ACPA)
chunk.topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
chunk.text: Testing concrete sewer and storm pipe, summarized from the American Concrete Pipe Association installation manual. Infiltration test: only meaningful when groundwater is at least 2 feet over the crown; the manual's base allowance is 200 gallons per inch of diameter per mile per day at 6 feet of head, rising to 282 at 12 feet. Exfiltration test: base head 3 feet; single reaches can run over if the project average passes. Low-pressure air test follows ASTM C924 and is limited to pipe 24 inch and smaller; it finds construction defects but does not measure water leakage. Larger pipe is tested one joint at a time with air or water under ASTM C1103. Vacuum testing: ASTM C1214 for pipe 4 to 36 inch, ASTM C1244 for manholes. Visual inspection looks for debris, cracks, joints fully home and sealed, smooth inverts and properly set frames. The project spec sets the pass numbers; many agencies allow far less leakage than 200 gallons (the Ten States figure is 100).
chunk.source: American Concrete Pipe Association, Concrete Pipe and Box Culvert Installation manual (our summary; read 2026-11-20). Standard Installations are the ones in ASTM C1479 and ASCE 15.

chunk.title: Clay pipe (VCP) bedding classes and load factors, ASTM C12
chunk.topic: Pipe installation guides by material
chunk.text: Vitrified clay pipe is installed under ASTM C12. Clay is rigid pipe, so the bedding class sets how much load the pipe can carry: the pipe's bearing strength is multiplied by the bedding load factor. Load factors published by the National Clay Pipe Institute from ASTM C12: Class D (flat trench bottom, least support) 1.1; Class C 1.5; Class B 1.9; crushed stone encasement 2.2; controlled low-strength material (CLSM, flowable fill) 2.8; concrete cradle 3.4. The plans call out the class; a crew that builds Class C where Class B was designed has cut the pipe's safe load by about a fifth. Shape bell holes so the barrel, not the bell, carries the load, and haunch the pipe by shovel slicing. Ten States Standards (33.83) point to these same ASTM C12 classes for rigid sewer pipe.
chunk.source: National Clay Pipe Institute bedding sheet (2021), load factors from ASTM C12, Standard Practice for Installing Vitrified Clay Pipe Lines (our summary; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Georgia GDOT storm drain pipe: video and laser inspection, 5 and 7.5 percent deflection (Section 550)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Georgia (GDOT Section 550, Storm Drain Pipe, Pipe-Arch Culverts, and Side Drain Pipe, supplemental specification revised 2015). Foundation and backfill follow Section 207 and Georgia Standards 1030D and 1030P. Thermoplastic pipe outside the roadbed in fills up to 10 feet uses Class II B2 or better soil for HDPE and Class II B3 or better for PVC and polypropylene; above 10 feet, graded aggregate (550.3.03). Thermoplastic joints are at least silt tight (550.3.05.C). Post-installation inspection (550.3.06): once compacted backfill reaches 8 feet or final cover is complete, with at least seven days notice to the Engineer; low-distortion video with laser profiling of 100 percent of storm drain pipe and at least 10 percent of side drain pipe on state route projects, by NASSCO PACP certified operators; manual inspection is allowed in pipe over 48 inches. Deflection over 5 percent of nominal diameter needs an evaluation by a Professional Engineer; over 7.5 percent is remediated or replaced. Joint separation over 1 inch must be fixed. Lift thickness and compaction percent are not confirmed here (they are not in Section 550); see Section 207.
chunk.source: Georgia DOT Supplemental Specification Section 550, Storm Drain Pipe, Pipe-Arch Culverts, and Side Drain Pipe (revised 2015; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Kentucky KYTC culvert and storm sewer pipe: bedding, 6-inch lifts, 95 percent, 48 inches cover (Section 701)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Kentucky (KYTC Standard Specifications, Section 701, culvert pipe, entrance pipe and storm sewer pipe). Bedding: No. 8 or No. 9-M stone or fine aggregate; do not use DGA or gravel base (701.02.04). Backfill in 6-inch lifts compacted to not less than 95 percent of maximum density by Kentucky Method KM 64-511 (701.03.06). Keep construction equipment and traffic off the pipe until there is 48 inches of cover over it (701.03.07). Joints are soil tight and wrapped with geotextile; concrete pipe joints may be mortar (1 cement to 2 sand), asphalt mastic, rubber gaskets or butyl sealant, with tied joints within 12 feet of the outlet on slopes 3:1 or steeper; metal pipe bands are at least 12 inches wide for pipe 54 inches and smaller; thermoplastic pipe uses bell and spigot with elastomeric seals (701.03.05). Trench limits are on the Standard Drawings.
chunk.source: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, Division 700, Sections 701, 705, 706, as posted by KYTC (edition year not shown in the file; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Kentucky KYTC pipeline camera inspection, mandrel and deflection pay cuts (Section 705); boring and jacking (706)
chunk.topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
chunk.text: Kentucky (KYTC Standard Specifications, Section 705, pipeline inspection). Installed pipe gets a camera inspection under Kentucky Method KM 64-114, with at least 24 hours notice to the Engineer, 30 days or more after earthwork is complete to within 1 foot of finished subgrade (705.02). Flexible pipe up to 48 inches can be checked with a mandrel that has at least 9 legs (705.03). Deflection table (705.05): 0 to 5.0 percent, full payment; 5.1 to 9.9 percent, 50 percent payment; 10 percent or greater, remove and replace. Section 706, boring and jacking: access pits on both sides, guide rails kept to line and grade, casing fitted tight to the bore with continuous welds. Minimum steel casing wall: 0.375 inch for 18 inch and smaller, 0.500 inch for 24 to 30 inch, 0.532 inch for 36 inch, 0.625 inch for 42 inch (706.02.01).
chunk.source: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, Division 700, Sections 701, 705, 706, as posted by KYTC (edition year not shown in the file; read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Iowa DOT corrugated metal and plastic culverts: cover and the 5 percent deflection test (Section 2417)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Iowa (Iowa DOT Standard Specifications, Section 2417, Corrugated Culverts, online version revised 10/20/2026). Corrugated metal or polyethylene roadway culverts get Class B bedding as shown in the contract documents (2417.03.C.1). Minimum cover: 1 foot over entrance culverts and 2 feet over roadway culverts; if construction traffic will cross, roadway culvert cover goes up to the pipe's nominal diameter or 3 feet, whichever is greater (2417.03.B). Polyethylene pipe deflection test (2417.03.C.2): at least 10 percent of locations, no sooner than 30 calendar days after backfill and before paving; the inside diameter may not shrink more than 5.0 percent; pipe 30 inches and smaller is tested with a nine-point mandrel, larger pipe is checked along its whole length. City street and utility work in Iowa usually follows SUDAS instead of the DOT book.
chunk.source: Iowa DOT Standard Specifications (current online General Supplemental series, page revised 10/20/2026), Section 2417 Corrugated Culverts (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Montana MDT culverts, storm drains and sewers: 6-inch lifts and 4 feet of cover before heavy equipment (Section 603)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Montana (MDT Standard Specifications, 2025 book, Section 603, Culverts, Storm Drains, Sanitary Sewers). Bedding is placed per Section 207 and the Detailed Drawings, with material tamped firmly under the pipe haunches (603.03.2, 603.04.3(B)). Backfill goes in layers of 6 inches loose thickness or less, to the moisture and density required by Subsection 203.03.3 (the percent is set there, not in 603). Heavy equipment stays off until cover is at least 4 feet or one-half the pipe diameter, whichever is greater (603.03.4(A)). Round concrete pipe joints are watertight with rubber gaskets (603.03.3(A)); siphon and irrigation pipe get a water-tightness test (MT 420); manhole connections follow ASTM C923. Section 604, manholes and inlets: backfill in loose layers of 6 inches or less, foundation compacted for full bearing.
chunk.source: Montana DOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, 2025 redline book, Sections 603 and 604 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Wyoming WYDOT culvert excavation and backfill: 8-inch lifts at 95 percent (Section 206)
chunk.topic: Spec books: trench, bedding, backfill and compaction
chunk.text: Wyoming (WYDOT 2021 Standard Specifications, Section 206, Excavation and Backfill for Culverts). Backfill in loose layers of about 8 inches, each compacted to at least 95.0 percent of maximum density at moisture between plus 2 and minus 4 percent of optimum (206.4.5.1). Compact the last 6 inches below structures or bedding to at least 95.0 percent (206.4.4). Over water and sewer lines, hand-place the first 12 inches. Do not backfill against cast-in-place boxes until 14 calendar days or 80 percent of design strength. Flowable fill: at least 12 inches over the conduit and no vehicle loads until 24 hours after it sets (206.4.5.3). Pipe bedding and laying are in Section 603 (603.4.4 and 603.4.5). Section 212, structure backfill: loose layers of about 8 inches compacted to the density of the adjacent material, placed evenly on both sides.
chunk.source: Wyoming DOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, 2021 edition, Sections 206 and 212 (read 2026-11-20; Section 603 not read)

chunk.title: Arizona ADOT pipe culverts and storm drains (Section 501) and the 2027 spec book change
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Arizona (ADOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction). Edition: the 2021 edition is in use now; ADOT says the 2027 edition applies to all projects advertising on and after January 4, 2027, electronic only, so check which book your contract names. Section 501, Pipe Culvert and Storm Drains, as described in ADOT's own Construction Manual (March 2025): a written trenching plan is required for trenches deeper than 5 feet (501-1); trench widths and the minimum 1 foot of cover are on Standard Drawing C-13.15, and cover must be increased for construction traffic, which is the contractor's responsibility (501-3.01); pipe 36 inches and larger in a trench is bedded in cement-treated slurry from the trench bottom to the springline (501-3.04); replacement backfill is compacted to 95 percent of maximum density (501-3.07(B)). The manual advises inspectors that heavy vibratory equipment should not run directly over pipe until there is at least 3 feet of cover and that nothing should be placed on flowable fill for 24 hours. In the Phoenix area, city and county work usually follows the MAG Uniform Standard Specifications instead.
chunk.source: ADOT Construction Manual, Chapter 5, Sections 501-505 (March 2025), describing the ADOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction; edition notice at azdot.gov/business/contracts-and-specifications (both read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas, Fort Worth utility trench spec: embedment, 12-inch lifts, 95 and 98 percent, test frequency (33 05 10)
chunk.topic: Spec books: trench, bedding, backfill and compaction
chunk.text: Texas, City of Fort Worth (Standard Specification 33 05 10, Utility Trench Excavation, Embedment and Backfill, revised April 2, 2021). Embedment and initial backfill go 6 to 12 inches above the pipe for water lines and for sanitary sewer and HDPE storm pipe; reinforced concrete storm pipe is embedded to the spring line; polypropylene storm pipe gets crushed rock to the top of pipe (3.4.D). Embedment and initial backfill are compacted to 95 percent Standard Proctor (ASTM D698). Final backfill: loose lifts of 12 inches or less; 95 percent under existing or future pavement less than 15 feet deep, 98 percent for select fill 15 feet and deeper, 95 percent outside pavement; moisture from minus 2 to plus 5 percent of optimum (3.4.E.3). Density tests: at least one per 2 vertical feet of compacted backfill and at least every 200 feet of trench, staggered by lift (3.7.A.2.d). Water lines 12 inch and smaller: top of pipe at least 42 inches below proposed grade unless the drawings say otherwise. Trench safety follows OSHA Subpart P and an Excavation Safety Plan designed by a Texas-licensed engineer. Other cities in the area use the NCTCOG specifications.
chunk.source: City of Fort Worth Standard Specification 33 05 10, Utility Trench Excavation, Embedment and Backfill, revised April 2, 2021 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Texas water and sewer separation: the 9-foot rule (TCEQ 30 TAC 217.53 and 290.44)
chunk.topic: Water and sewer separation distances
chunk.text: Texas uses 9 feet, not 10. TCEQ rules: sewer pipe and manholes should be at least 9 feet from water lines, in a separate trench and below the water line where possible (30 TAC 217.53(d); 30 TAC 290.44(e)(1)). When 9 feet cannot be met, parallel lines: the water line at least 2 feet above and 4 feet to the side of the sewer, with 150 psi pressure-rated sewer pipe, or encasement (217.53(d)(6); 290.44(e)(4)(A)). Sewer crossing under a water line: 150 psi pipe with at least 6 inches of separation, one length at least 18 feet long centered on the water line; or other pipe with at least 2 feet of separation and cement-stabilized sand; or a casing pipe at least two sizes larger with spacers no more than 5 feet apart (217.53(d)(7)). A manhole within 9 feet of a water line must pass the leak test or get at least 1 foot of cement-stabilized sand. Water lines: at least 24 inches of cover, 35 psi minimum pressure, fire hydrants not within 9 feet of sewer lines, new mains disinfected per AWWA C651 with at least one bacteria sample per 1,000 feet (290.44).
chunk.source: 30 Texas Administrative Code 217.53 (TCEQ, wastewater collection pipe design; amended eff. 12/4/2015) and 30 TAC 290.44 (water distribution), read at law.cornell.edu 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Florida water main separation from sewer, storm and reclaimed lines (Rule 62-555.314)
chunk.topic: Water and sewer separation distances
chunk.text: Florida has its own separation numbers (F.A.C. Rule 62-555.314, amended effective 2/26/2025). Side by side, a new or relocated water main is at least: 3 feet from storm sewers, stormwater force mains and regulated reclaimed water lines; 3 feet, preferably 10, from vacuum sanitary sewers; 6 feet, preferably 10, from gravity or pressure sanitary sewers and wastewater force mains (gravity sewer can come down to 3 feet if the bottom of the water main is at least 6 inches above the top of the sewer); 10 feet from onsite sewage (septic) systems. Crossing a gravity or vacuum sewer or storm sewer: water main at least 6 inches, preferably 12, above, or at least 12 inches below; above is preferred. Crossing a pressure sewer, force main or reclaimed line: at least 12 inches above or below. At crossings, center one full length of water main, or keep water main joints at least 3 feet from storm and vacuum sewer joints and 6 feet from sanitary sewer and force main joints. No water main may pass through or touch a sanitary sewer manhole. The Department can allow exceptions with extra protection such as pressure-rated sewer pipe, a casing or concrete encasement.
chunk.source: Florida Administrative Code Rule 62-555.314, Location of Public Water System Mains (amended eff. 2/26/2025), read at law.cornell.edu 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Florida FDOT Standard Specifications: which edition is in force (July-to-June books)
chunk.topic: Spec books: which edition applies
chunk.text: Florida (FDOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction). FDOT publishes a new eBook each fiscal year: the FY 2026-27 book took effect July 1, 2026 and the FY 2027-28 book takes effect July 1, 2027; your contract names the one that applies. The sections a pipe crew lives in are Section 125 (Excavation for Structures and Pipe), Section 430 (Pipe Culverts) and Section 425 (Inlets, Manholes, and Junction Boxes), with jack and bore in Section 556. The numbers in those sections are not confirmed in this library (the files would not open here), so for lift thickness, density and pipe inspection go to the book itself at fdot.gov/specifications. County and city utility work in Florida usually follows the utility's own standards, and water main separation follows state Rule 62-555.314.
chunk.source: FDOT Standard Specification Library, fdot.gov/specifications/standard-specification-library (edition list read 2026-11-20); section numbers not re-read

chunk.title: Indiana INDOT pipe: mandrel testing of plastic pipe, Section 715
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Indiana (INDOT Standard Specifications Section 715, Pipe Culverts, and Storm and Sanitary Sewers, as changed by Recurring Special Provision 715-R-809 dated 09-01-26). After the visual or video inspection, plastic pipe is mandrel tested: corrugated and smooth-wall polyethylene, corrugated polypropylene, and profile and smooth-wall PVC. The Engineer picks the runs, and at least 10 percent of the total length of each material is tested; underdrain pipe is exempt. Backfill for corrugated pipe may not have particles larger than half the corrugation depth. Thermoplastic and metal pipe must come from INDOT's qualified products list. The deflection limit, lift thickness and compaction numbers are in the base Section 715 and Section 211 text, which was not read here, so those numbers are not confirmed.
chunk.source: INDOT Recurring Special Provision 715-R-809, Pipe Culverts, and Storm and Sanitary Sewers, dated 09-01-26 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: North Dakota NDDOT culverts and storm drains: 6-inch lifts, 90 percent, 95 percent mandrel (Section 714)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: North Dakota (NDDOT 2023 Standard Specifications, Section 714, Culverts, Storm Drains, Edgedrains, and Underdrains). Bedding is tamped under both haunches up to 15 percent of the pipe height with hand-held air tampers (714.04 A.4). Backfill in lifts of 6 inches or less; aggregate backfill compacted to at least 90 percent of maximum dry density at 2 points below to 3 points above optimum moisture (714.04 A.10 and A.11). Cover before equipment crosses: the book gives no number and sends you to the pipe maker's recommendation (714.04 A.12). Deflection test: metal and thermoplastic pipe under mainline and paved crossroads is tested at least 30 days after installation with a nine-point mandrel at least 95 percent of the inside diameter; pipe the mandrel will not pass is replaced (714.04 A.8). Concrete pipe joints are wrapped in geotextile. Jacked steel pipe: bore without water, start within 0.1 foot of staked grade, and stay within 1/2 foot of line and grade (714.04 C). Manholes and inlets (722): backfill lifts of 6 inches or less at 90 percent. Water and sewer lines (724): bedding up the sides to one-third of the pipe diameter, backfill in 6-inch loose lifts.
chunk.source: North Dakota DOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, 2023, Sections 714, 722, 724 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: Ohio ODOT pipe culverts and sewers: installation plan, 7.5 percent deflection, 30 to 90 day inspection (Item 611)
chunk.topic: Spec books: culvert and storm drain pipe installation
chunk.text: Ohio (ODOT Construction and Material Specifications, Item 611, Pipe Culverts, Sewers, Drains, and Drainage Structures). These numbers are from the 2013 online edition; the current 2023 book was not checked, so treat them as not confirmed for a current job and read Item 611 in the contract's edition. In Item 611 the contractor's installation plan sets trench dimensions, bedding, lift thickness and compaction (611.04, 611.06); rock or unsuitable material is removed at least 6 inches below the pipe and replaced with structural backfill; if no bedding is used, the middle third of the bed is loosened. With low-strength mortar bedding, the mortar backfill is carried at least 6 inches over the conduit. Performance inspection (611.12): for runs over 20 feet, 30 to 90 days after finished grade, with 5 workdays notice to the Engineer and a video record. Metal and plastic conduit is repaired or replaced if the mandrel will not pass or the laser profile shows more than 7.5 percent deflection (611.13). Sanitary concrete pipe joints are tested under ASTM C969 or C1103. Structure inverts must be within 0.1 foot or 5 percent of the pipe diameter, whichever is greater (611.14).
chunk.source: Ohio DOT Construction and Material Specifications, Item 611, 2013 online edition (read 2026-11-20). The current book is the 2023 C&MS with yearly updates, which was not read.

chunk.title: Nevada NDOT Standard Specifications: current edition and where pipe work is covered
chunk.topic: Spec books: which edition applies
chunk.text: Nevada (NDOT Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction). NDOT lists the 2024 edition as current. The numbers for pipe culverts, structure excavation and backfill in the 2024 book are not confirmed in this library because the file would not open; get them from the book on NDOT's Standard Specifications and Plans page or from the NDOT Specifications office. In the Las Vegas valley, city, county and water district work normally follows the Uniform Standard Specifications and Drawings for Clark County instead, and in the Reno area the Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (the Orange Book), each with the agency's own amendments. Your contract says which book governs.
chunk.source: Nevada DOT, Standard Specifications, Standard Plans, and Design Guides page (edition list read 2026-11-20; the 2024 book itself would not open)

chunk.title: Utah UDOT Standard Specifications: editions listed and where city work differs
chunk.topic: Spec books: which edition applies
chunk.text: Utah (UDOT Standard Specifications). UDOT's standards page lists yearly books, with 2027 the newest listed above 2026 and 2025; the contract names the one that applies. The numbers in UDOT's drainage pipe and backfill sections are not confirmed in this library because the files would not open; read the section in the contract's edition on UDOT's standards page or ask the UDOT Standards Coordinator. City, county and district utility work along the Wasatch Front usually follows the APWA Utah Chapter Manual of Standard Specifications and Plans with local amendments, not the UDOT book.
chunk.source: UDOT Standard Specifications and Standard Drawings page (edition list read 2026-11-20; the books are in an online folder that would not open)

chunk.title: Oregon ODOT 2024 book: effective date, video speed, boring and jacking, adjusting manholes
chunk.topic: Spec books: jacking, boring and tunneling
chunk.text: Oregon (2024 Oregon Standard Specifications for Construction). This edition applies to ODOT projects bid on or after Dec. 1, 2023, and many cities use it with their own special provisions. Trench width at the surface is as narrow as practical but not less than 24 inches (00405.41(c)); the pipe zone runs to at least 8 inches over the pipe (00405.02); trench backfill is 95 percent of AASHTO T 99 under roadway and shoulders and 90 percent elsewhere (00405.46(c)(2)). Video inspection: the camera moves no faster than 30 feet per minute while recording (00445.74). Deflection mandrel: at least 9 vanes, 95 percent of the pipe's initial inside diameter, not less than 30 days after backfill (00445.73(c)). Tunneling, boring and jacking (Section 00406): pipe, casing or sleeves are jacked or bored to the required line and grade, and jacked casings 36 inches and larger get grout nipples at 10-foot centers when pressure grouting is specified (00406.12). Manhole vacuum test: 10 inches of mercury, timed to 9 inches (00470.71(b)). Adjusting structures (00490.46): no more than 24 inches from the new frame grade to the top of the cone.
chunk.source: Oregon Standard Specifications for Construction, 2024 (ODOT/APWA Oregon Chapter), Sections 00405, 00406, 00445, 00470, 00490 (read 2026-11-20)

chunk.title: When a crew truck needs a CDL: the 26,001 lb and 10,000 lb trailer rule (Class A, B, C)
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: A commercial driver license (CDL) is needed by weight rating, not by what the truck looks like (49 CFR 383.5). Class A (combination): the truck and trailer together are rated or weigh 26,001 lb or more AND the trailer is rated or weighs more than 10,000 lb. Class B (heavy straight truck): the single truck is rated or weighs 26,001 lb or more, for example most tandem dump trucks and water trucks. Class C: smaller vehicles built for 16 or more people including the driver, or hauling placarded hazardous materials. The rule uses whichever is greater, the rating on the door tag (GVWR) or the real weight. The combination rating (GCWR) is the greater of the maker's number on the power unit's label or the truck GVWR plus the trailer GVWR. Worked example: a pickup tagged 14,000 lb GVWR pulling an equipment trailer tagged 14,000 lb is 28,000 lb combined with a trailer over 10,000 lb, so it is a Class A combination. The same pickup with a 9,900 lb trailer is 23,900 lb and needs no CDL. A 25,999 lb straight truck with a trailer of 10,000 lb or less needs no CDL either. States issue the license and may add their own rules, and some state exemptions exist, so check the state driver manual.
chunk.source: 49 CFR 383.5 (definitions: commercial motor vehicle Groups A, B, C; GCWR; GVWR)
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: The 10,001 lb line: when a pickup and trailer becomes a DOT commercial vehicle (no CDL needed)
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Two federal weight lines get mixed up. 26,001 lb is the CDL line. 10,001 lb is the "commercial motor vehicle" line for the safety rules. 49 CFR 390.5 says a commercial motor vehicle is a vehicle "used on a highway in interstate commerce to transport passengers or property" that has a "gross vehicle weight rating or gross combination weight rating, or gross vehicle weight or gross combination weight, of 4,536 kg (10,001 pounds) or more, whichever is greater". So a 1 ton pickup pulling a mini excavator is usually over 10,001 lb combined, with no CDL needed. Above that line the driver and truck come under the federal motor carrier safety rules that use this definition: a medical card (49 CFR 391.45), hours of service (Part 395), load checks (392.9), daily defect reports and a yearly inspection (Part 396), and a USDOT number on the truck. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.source: 49 CFR 390.5 (definition of commercial motor vehicle, 10,001 lb); 49 CFR 383.5 (26,001 lb CDL line)
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Do we need a DOT number (USDOT number) on our pickups and work trucks, even if we only work in state
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: FMCSA says a company needs a USDOT number when it runs a vehicle in interstate commerce that has a weight rating or weight "of 4,536 kg (10,001 pounds) or more, whichever is greater" (truck alone or truck plus trailer), or carries placarded hazardous materials. Interstate means trade that crosses a state line, "Between a place in a State and a place outside of such State". For companies that stay inside one state, FMCSA lists the states that also require a USDOT number for in-state commercial trucks: AL, AK, AZ, CA, CO, CT, DE, FL, GA, HI, ID, IN, IA, KS, KY, ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, MO, MT, NE, NV, NJ, NY, NC, OH, OK, OR, PA, SC, TX, UT, WA, WV, WI, WY, plus Puerto Rico. Each of those states sets its own weight line for in-state trucks, so check with the state. A state not on the list may still have its own state number or permit. The number is free from FMCSA and is tied to the company, not to each truck. The list is from the FMCSA page as updated September 3, 2025.
chunk.source: FMCSA, "Do I Need a USDOT Number?" (page updated 2025-09-03); 49 CFR 390.5
chunk.edition: FMCSA web page, last updated September 3, 2025

chunk.title: DOT medical card: who needs one and how often (every 24 months)
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: A driver of a commercial motor vehicle (10,001 lb or more in interstate commerce, with or without a CDL) must be medically examined and certified by a medical examiner. 49 CFR 391.45 requires a new exam for any driver who has not been certified "during the preceding 24 months". Some drivers are on a 12 month cycle instead: drivers with insulin-treated diabetes, drivers certified under the alternative vision standard, and drivers in an exempt intracity zone. A driver whose ability to do the job has been affected by an injury or illness must be examined again before driving, whatever the date on the card. A medical examiner can also write a card for less than 24 months to watch a condition such as high blood pressure. So the pipelayer who only drives the 1 ton with the equipment trailer needs a current medical card, not just the CDL drivers. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.source: 49 CFR 391.45 (persons who must be medically examined and certified); 49 CFR 390.5
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Hours of service for truck drivers: 11 hours driving, 14 hour day, 30 minute break, 60/70 hours
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Federal hours of service for property-carrying commercial trucks (49 CFR 395.3): 10 hours off first: "A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty". 14 hour window: a driver may not drive after 14 consecutive hours from coming on duty. Breaks do not stop that clock. 11 hours driving: "A driver may drive a total of 11 hours" inside the 14 hour window. 30 minute break: no driving once more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a 30 minute interruption (off duty, or on duty not driving). Short-haul drivers are excused. Weekly: no driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 days (company does not run every day) or 70 hours in 8 days (company runs every day). Restart: 34 or more consecutive hours off duty resets the 7 or 8 day count. Unexpected bad weather or traffic allows up to 2 more hours (395.1(b)(1)). The limits stop the driving, not the work. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Short-haul exception: no logbook inside 150 air miles (time cards instead)
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Most pipe crews need no logbook because of the short-haul exception, 49 CFR 395.1(e). CDL drivers, 395.1(e)(1): no log is needed on a day when the driver stays "within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location", returns there and is released within 14 consecutive hours, and has at least 10 hours off before the next shift. Drivers of trucks that do not need a CDL, 395.1(e)(2): stay within 150 air miles and return to the normal reporting location at the end of each shift; they may not drive after the 14th hour on duty on 5 days of any 7, and may go to the 16th hour on 2 days of the 7. The company keeps time records for 6 months (time in, time out, total hours each day). The 11 hour driving limit and the 60/70 hour weekly limits still apply. On a day the driver goes past the radius or the hours, a regular log is required. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Construction and utility truck exceptions to hours of service: the 24 hour restart
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Two federal hours-of-service exceptions are written for our kind of work. Construction materials and equipment, 49 CFR 395.1(m): for a driver mainly hauling construction materials and equipment, "any period of 7 or 8 consecutive days may end with the beginning of any off-duty period of 24 or more successive hours." So the weekly 60 or 70 hour count restarts after 24 hours off instead of 34. The definition (395.2) covers hauling "to or from an active construction site" "within a 75 air mile radius of the normal work reporting location of the driver"; a state may set 50 to 75 air miles for in-state moves. Utility service vehicles, 395.1(n): the hours-of-service part does not apply at all to drivers of a utility service vehicle, which 395.2 defines as a commercial vehicle used to repair, maintain or operate utility facilities and "operated primarily within the service area of a utility's subscribers or consumers". That fits a utility's own service trucks and contractors doing that repair and maintenance work; whether a truck on new-construction pipe work qualifies is not confirmed here, so ask the state DOT enforcement office before relying on it.
chunk.source: 49 CFR 395.1(m), 395.1(n); 49 CFR 395.2 (definitions)
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20
chunk.unconfirmed: whether new-construction pipe crews fit the utility service vehicle definition

chunk.title: Do hours laying pipe count against a driver's 14 hours? What "on duty" means
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Yes. For a worker who also drives a commercial truck (10,001 lb or more), time spent working in the trench counts as on-duty time. 49 CFR 395.2 says on-duty time "means all time from the time a driver begins to work or is required to be in readiness to work" until relieved. It includes driving, servicing the truck, loading, and "any other work for a motor carrier". The 14 hour rule in 395.3 says a driver may not drive after 14 consecutive hours from coming on duty. Put together: a pipelayer who clocks in at 6:00 am, lays pipe all day, and is still on the job at 8:00 pm cannot legally drive the equipment truck and trailer back to the yard, unless the 16 hour short-haul day for non-CDL trucks applies (allowed on 2 days in 7, see 395.1(e)(2)). Someone inside their hours has to drive, or the truck stays. The weekly 60 or 70 hour count includes the trench hours too. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Electronic logs (ELD): which crew trucks do not need one
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: FMCSA lists the drivers who do not have to use an electronic logging device (ELD): drivers using the short-haul exception ("Drivers who use the short-haul, timecard exceptions are not required to keep records of duty status (RODS) or use ELDs."); drivers who have to keep a log on no more than 8 days in any 30 day period (they can use a paper log on those days); driveaway-towaway operations where the vehicle driven is the thing being delivered; and trucks "manufactured before the model year 2000". A crew truck that normally stays inside 150 air miles and gets back within the short-haul hours needs time cards, not an ELD. If that truck goes outside the exception more than 8 days in any 30, it needs an ELD. The FMCSA page was issued as guidance in 2018 and marked rescinded on March 10, 2022 only because the same rules are in the regulation itself (49 CFR 395.8 and Part 395 Subpart B); the regulation text was not re-read for this chunk.
chunk.source: FMCSA, "Who is exempt from the ELD rule?" (guidance 2018; 49 CFR 395.8(a)(1)(iii))

chunk.title: Pre-trip and post-trip truck inspection (DVIR): what the driver must do
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Before driving: 49 CFR 396.13 says "Before driving a motor vehicle, the driver shall" "Be satisfied that the motor vehicle is in safe operating condition", review the last inspection report if one was required, and sign it. End of day: 396.11 requires a written report "at the completion of each day's work on each vehicle operated" covering at least brakes (including trailer brake connections), steering, lights, tires, horn, wipers, mirrors, coupling devices, wheels and emergency equipment. But: "Drivers are not required to prepare a report if no defect or deficiency is discovered by or reported to the driver." The company must fix safety defects before the truck goes out again, certify it on the report, and keep it "for three months from the date the written report was prepared." The trailer is part of the inspection. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Annual DOT inspection: every truck AND trailer, proof on the vehicle
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: 49 CFR 396.17: "Every commercial motor vehicle must be inspected as required by this section." In a combination each unit counts on its own: "the tractor, semitrailer, and the full trailer (including the converter dolly if so equipped) must each be inspected." A commercial vehicle may not be used unless each part of it "has passed an inspection in accordance with the terms of this section at least once during the preceding 12 months" and "documentation of such inspection is on the vehicle." The proof can be the inspection report itself or a sticker or decal showing the inspection date, who did it, the vehicle it belongs to, and that it passed. What crews miss: the equipment trailer and the tilt-deck need their own inspection and their own sticker, not just the truck. This applies from the 10,001 lb commercial vehicle line, not only to CDL trucks. A roadside officer will ask for the sticker or report on both units. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Hauling the excavator: stop and check chains and binders in the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: When hauling equipment, pipe or plates, the driver has to stop and check the chains, binders and straps. 49 CFR 392.9: a commercial truck may not be driven unless the cargo is "properly distributed and adequately secured", and the "tailgate, tailboard, doors, tarpaulins, spare tire and other equipment used in its operation" are secured, and nothing blocks the driver's view or movement. The driver must make sure of that before driving, then "Inspect the cargo and the devices used to secure the cargo within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip" and adjust or add tie-downs as needed. After that, re-check whenever the driver changes duty status, or the truck "has been driven for 3 hours", or "has been driven for 150 miles, whichever occurs first." For a crew this means: after loading the excavator, pipe, plates or a trench box, stop within the first 50 miles (chains and binders settle), and again at the fuel stop. Heavy equipment over 10,000 lb has its own tie-down rule (49 CFR 393.130: at least four tie-downs, see the library chunk on tying down equipment).
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Federal truck weight limits: 80,000 lb gross, 20,000 single axle, 34,000 tandem
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: On the Interstate system and reasonable access to it, 23 CFR 658.17 sets the weight limits a state must allow without a special permit: "The maximum gross vehicle weight shall be 80,000 pounds." One axle: 20,000 pounds. "The maximum gross weight on tandem axles is 34,000 pounds." Groups of axles must also meet the bridge formula, W = 500 x (LN / (N - 1) + 12N + 36), where W is the weight allowed on the group, L is the distance in feet between the outer axles of the group, and N is the number of axles. Two sets of tandems may each carry 34,000 lb when the first and last axles are at least 36 ft apart. Anything heavier, such as a large excavator on a lowboy, moves on a state overweight permit, and the permit sets the route, the hours and the escorts. States also have their own limits on state and local roads, bridge postings, and seasonal (frost) load limits, which can be lower. Axle weights are what get a dump truck ticketed: a truck can be under its gross and still be over on the rear tandem if the load sits too far back.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Hauling gas cans and diesel on the crew truck: the materials of trade rule
chunk.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
chunk.text: Fuel a crew carries for its own saws and pumps is a "material of trade": under 49 CFR 173.6 no placards or shipping papers are needed inside these limits. Gasoline (a Class 3 flammable liquid, Packing Group II): each container no more than "30 L (8 gallons)". All materials of trade on the truck together: no more than "200 kg (440 pounds)" gross weight. "For gasoline, a packaging must be made of metal or plastic" and meet the OSHA safety can rules (29 CFR 1910.106(d)(2) or 1926.152(a)(1)) or DOT packaging rules. Cans must be closed, secured and marked "gasoline". The driver "must be informed of the presence of the hazardous material" and of these limits. Diesel: a liquid with a flash point at or above 100 F "may be reclassed as a combustible liquid" (173.150(f)(1)), and the hazardous materials rules "do not apply to a material classed as a combustible liquid in a non-bulk packaging" (173.150(f)(2)). A large diesel transfer tank is bulk packaging and has marking and placard rules. The gallon size where a tank becomes bulk is in 49 CFR 171.8 and was not confirmed for this chunk, so check before buying a tank.
chunk.source: 49 CFR 173.6 (materials of trade); 49 CFR 173.150(f) (combustible liquids)
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20
chunk.unconfirmed: the gallon figure that separates non-bulk from bulk packaging (49 CFR 171.8) was not read

chunk.title: How big a job needs a stormwater permit and SWPPP: 1 acre. And where EPA's own permit applies
chunk.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
chunk.text: Federal rule of thumb: a job that will disturb one or more acres of land needs stormwater permit coverage before dirt moves, and so does a smaller job that is part of a larger common plan (a phase of a subdivision, for example) that will disturb an acre or more in total (EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, Part 1.1.2). A long trench adds up: width disturbed times length. In most states the state environmental agency issues the permit, with its own name, forms and fees. EPA's own permit (the CGP) is used only where EPA is the permitting authority (Part 1.1.3, Appendix B): all of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the Pacific territories, plus Indian country in most states and many federal facilities and lands of exclusive federal jurisdiction. On an EPA job the Notice of Intent goes in "At least 14 calendar days before commencing construction activities." The 2022 CGP expires at 11:59 pm on February 16, 2027. EPA proposed a 2027 CGP on August 3, 2026; as of EPA's page dated November 17, 2026 it was not final. On a tribal or federal job in any state, ask which permit covers the site before assuming it is the state one.
chunk.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 1.1.2, 1.1.3, 1.4.3, Appendix B; EPA proposed 2027 CGP page (updated 2026-11-17)
chunk.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

chunk.title: How often the SWPPP inspection is due: every 7 days, or 14 days plus after a 0.25 inch rain
chunk.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
chunk.text: Under EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit the site picks one inspection schedule (Part 4.2): either "At least once every seven (7) calendar days", or once every 14 calendar days plus within 24 hours of a storm of 0.25 inches or more in 24 hours (or snowmelt that causes a discharge). Sites draining to sensitive waters inspect every 7 days and within 24 hours of such a storm (Part 4.3). Fewer are allowed for stabilized areas, arid areas in the dry season, and frozen ground (Part 4.4). The inspector must be a "qualified person": for projects covered on or after February 17, 2023, someone who has passed EPA's construction inspection course and exam or holds a current equivalent certification (Parts 4.1, 6.3). Fixes have a clock: a new or replaced control or a significant repair within 7 calendar days; routine maintenance by the close of the next business day (Part 5.2.1). These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
chunk.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 4.1 to 4.4, 5.2.1, 6.3
chunk.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

chunk.title: Stabilization deadline (14 days), silt fence clean-out at half height, concrete washout
chunk.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
chunk.text: Three field rules from EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit. Stabilization (Part 2.2.14): where earth work has stopped for good, or will sit idle for 14 or more days, start stabilizing right away (seed and mulch, blanket, rock, pavement) and finish "as soon as practicable, but no later than 14 calendar days" after starting, on sites with 5 acres or less disturbed at one time. Sites with more than 5 acres open at once, and sites draining to sensitive waters, get 7 calendar days. Perimeter controls (Part 2.2.3): silt fence, wattles and berms go in before the dirt work upslope; remove built-up sediment "before it has accumulated to one-half of the above-ground height of any perimeter control." Concrete washout (Part 2.3.4): wash chutes, pumps and tools only into a "leak-proof container or leak-proof and lined pit"; never onto the ground, into a storm drain inlet, a ditch or the trench. Let it harden and haul it off. Paint, form oil and curing compound wash water are handled the same way. These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
chunk.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 2.2.3, 2.2.14 (Table 2), 2.3.4
chunk.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

chunk.title: Pumping the trench out to a ditch or storm drain: what to check (daily, no foam, no sheen, 50 NTU)
chunk.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
chunk.text: Pumping water out of a trench or excavation to a ditch, creek or storm drain (dewatering) is a regulated discharge under EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit. What the water must look like (Part 2.4): "Do not discharge visible floating solids or foam", and the discharge must not cause "a visible sheen on the water surface". Run the discharge through a sediment control (dewatering bag, weir tank, basin or thick vegetation) and do not let it erode where it lands. Inspection (Part 4.3.2): the dewatering operation is inspected "once per day on which the discharge occurs." If it shows a plume, sheen or foam, stop or cut the discharge right away and fix the cause before pumping again (Part 5.2.2). Sites that pump to sensitive waters must also sample the dewatering discharge for turbidity against a benchmark of 50 NTU (Part 3.3). Water that smells of fuel or has a sheen is not ordinary trench water: stop pumping and call the office. These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
chunk.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 2.4, 3.3, 4.3.2, 5.2.2
chunk.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

chunk.title: OSHA on tapping, cutting or removing asbestos-cement water pipe: Class II work, no "below the limit" exemption
chunk.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
chunk.text: OSHA letter of May 29, 2007 on tapping and tying in to asbestos-cement (AC, transite) water pipe under 29 CFR 1926.1101. A competent person must classify the work. OSHA said removal of AC pipe "is normally Class II asbestos work." It can be Class III only when it is repair or maintenance work that disturbs a small amount, no more than fits in one glove bag or waste bag. If it is not clear, the employer "should assume the higher class applies." Required: wet methods, HEPA vacuums, prompt cleanup and bagging of waste. Prohibited: high-speed abrasive disc saws without controls, compressed air, dry sweeping. In practice that means a snap cutter or a wet hand method, never a dry cut-off saw. Training: Class III workers need training that "shall take at least 16 hours" in the usual case; Class II workers need training with hands-on practice for the material and method. Being under the exposure limit does not exempt the work: a consultant "was in error when he stated that when an activity is below the PEL it is exempt". State rules can be stricter.
chunk.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, May 29, 2007 (29 CFR 1926.1101(b), (g), (k)(9), (o)(4))
chunk.edition: OSHA letter of interpretation dated May 29, 2007

chunk.title: EPA asbestos rule for AC pipe jobs: the 260 ft line, 10 working day notice, keep it wet
chunk.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
chunk.text: EPA's asbestos air rule (the Asbestos NESHAP, 40 CFR Part 61 Subpart M) can apply to a job that removes or breaks up asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe. The amounts that trigger the full notice and work-practice rules in 40 CFR 61.145 are "At least 80 linear meters (260 linear feet) on pipes", or 160 square feet on other components. Above the line, written notice goes to the air agency "At least 10 working days before asbestos stripping or removal work or any other activity begins". Work practices: "Adequately wet the material and ensure that it remains wet until collected and contained", and no visible dust to the outside air. EPA describes the normal way to take out AC pipe as open trench: expose it, and it is "wet-cut into 6- and 8-foot sections using a snap cutter or similar tool", wrapped, and hauled to a landfill that takes asbestos waste. "All ACWM must be kept adequately wet and sealed in leak-tight containers." A short tie-in on one stick is normally under the 260 ft line, but OSHA's worker rules apply at any length. State and local air agencies often have lower thresholds.
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Pipe bursting asbestos-cement pipe: EPA has not approved it as an alternative (2019 notice)
chunk.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
chunk.text: Pipe bursting or reaming an old asbestos-cement (AC, transite) main breaks the pipe into fragments and leaves them in the ground. In its Federal Register notice of June 10, 2019 (84 FR 26852) EPA said it "neither approved pipe bursting nor pipe reaming as AWPs to replace A/C pipe" (AWP means alternative work practice). EPA said bursting or reaming more than the threshold amount of AC pipe has to follow the Asbestos NESHAP, including the standards for an active asbestos waste disposal site (40 CFR 61.154) and, where the broken pipe is left in the ground, the standards for an inactive site (40 CFR 61.151). In the same notice EPA approved one trenchless method, "close tolerance pipe slurrification (CTPS)", which grinds the old pipe into a wet slurry that is pumped out and disposed of as asbestos waste; it was approved on May 30, 2019 with required inspections, wetting, sampling and landfill disposal. So before bidding or starting a burst on an AC main, get the owner's and the air agency's position in writing. Some states have their own written policy on AC pipe bursting.
chunk.source: EPA, Notice of Final Approval: Alternative Work Practice Standard for Asbestos Cement Pipe Replacement, 84 FR 26852 (June 10, 2019)

chunk.title: Fuel or oil spill that reaches water: call the National Response Center, 1-800-424-8802
chunk.topic: Fuel and oil on the job: spill reporting and fuel storage rules
chunk.text: Federal rule (40 CFR Part 110, the "sheen rule"): an oil discharge to water must be reported when it is a harmful quantity, which EPA explains as oil that "violates state water quality standards, causes a film or sheen on the water's surface" or "leaves sludge or emulsion beneath the surface". Oil means diesel, gasoline, hydraulic and motor oil. There is no gallon minimum: a sheen on a creek, a lake, or a ditch or storm drain that leads to one is enough. The person in charge must notify the National Response Center "immediately after he or she has knowledge of the discharge": "1-800-424-8802 or 1-202-267-2675", staffed 24 hours by the Coast Guard. On the job: stop the source, keep it out of inlets and water with booms, pads or a dirt berm, and call the foreman and the office. Most states also require a call to the state spill line, often for spills on dry ground over a set number of gallons. Never wash a spill down or bury it.
chunk.source: EPA, 40 CFR Part 110 Discharge of Oil regulation FAQ ("When must I report an oil discharge to NRC?")
chunk.edition: EPA FAQ page read 2026-11-20 (rule: 40 CFR Part 110)

chunk.title: When a yard or job site needs an SPCC plan: more than 1,320 gallons of oil in tanks and drums
chunk.topic: Fuel and oil on the job: spill reporting and fuel storage rules
chunk.text: EPA's Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule, 40 CFR Part 112, generally applies to a site that stores oil and has a "total aggregate capacity of aboveground oil storage containers greater than 1,320 gallons" and that "Has the potential to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines." Oil includes diesel, gasoline, hydraulic and motor oil, and used oil. Count the capacity of the containers, not what is in them today: a 1,000 gallon diesel tank plus a 500 gallon tank is 1,500 gallons and is over the line. A covered site needs a written SPCC plan, secondary containment for bulk containers (a double-wall tank or a dike or tub that holds the contents), regular inspections, and trained people. An engineer must certify the plan if "total oil storage capacity exceeds 10,000 gallons"; at or below that the owner may be able to self-certify. For a pipe company this usually comes up at the yard. Which small containers count toward the 1,320 gallons (EPA's rule text counts containers of 55 gallons and up) was not confirmed from the rule text for this chunk.
chunk.source: EPA Region 9 SPCC compliance fact sheet (September 2025); 40 CFR Part 112
chunk.unconfirmed: the 55 gallon minimum container size for counting capacity (40 CFR 112.1) was not read in the rule text

chunk.title: Creek, ditch and wetland crossings: Corps of Engineers nationwide permits were reissued for 2026
chunk.topic: Working in or near streams and wetlands: Corps permits
chunk.text: Laying pipe across a stream, a wetland or some ditches is work in "waters of the United States" and needs authorization from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under the Clean Water Act (Section 404), usually through a nationwide permit (NWP) that the owner or engineer obtains before the job. The nationwide permits were reissued in 2026: the Corps published them in the Federal Register on January 8, 2026 ("The 56 reissued and one new nationwide permit in the final action"). "The nationwide permits in this action take effect March 15, 2026." "The 2021 permits are set to expire March 14, 2026." What this means on the job: the crossing has a permit with conditions that the crew has to follow, such as the limits of disturbance at the crossing, how the trench is backfilled and the bank restored, where spoil can go, and fish timing windows. Ask for the permit and its conditions before working at a crossing, and do not widen the work area on your own. A job permitted under the 2021 permits that was not finished may need its authorization checked against the 2026 permits; the terms of the 2026 utility line permits were not read for this chunk and are not confirmed here.
chunk.source: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers news release, January 8, 2026 (2026 nationwide permits; 91 FR, Jan. 8, 2026)
chunk.unconfirmed: terms and acreage limits of the 2026 utility line nationwide permits were not read

chunk.title: Certified payroll deadline on federal jobs: 7 days after payday, keep 3 years
chunk.topic: Prevailing wage paperwork: certified payroll and payment bonds
chunk.text: On Davis-Bacon (federally funded or assisted) construction, each contractor and subcontractor turns in a weekly certified payroll with a signed statement of compliance. 29 CFR 3.4 sets the deadline: the statement is delivered "within 7 days after the regular payment date of the payroll period". The 7 days run from the regular payday for that week, not from the end of the work week. It goes to the agency's representative at the site; if there is none, it is mailed or sent another reliable way to the agency contracting for or financing the work, inside the same 7 days. On most jobs the subcontractor sends it up through the prime contractor, who is responsible for all tiers, and many agencies now require their own online system. Records: the certified payrolls are kept for 3 years after all the work on the prime contract is completed, and the contractor keeps its own payroll records for the same time. A week with no work on the job is commonly reported as a "no work" payroll so the numbering stays continuous; check what the agency wants. State prevailing wage jobs have their own forms and deadlines (see the state chunks in the library).
chunk.source: 29 CFR 3.4 (submission of weekly statements and preservation and inspection of weekly payroll records)
chunk.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Chlorinating a new water main: tablet, continuous feed and slug doses and hold times (AWWA C651-14)
chunk.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
chunk.text: AWWA C651-14 gives three main ways to disinfect a new main. Tablet method (Sec. 4.3): calcium hypochlorite tablets glued in the top of each pipe as it is laid, for a dose of 25 mg/L; fill slowly, no faster than 1 ft per second; hold at least 24 hours, or 48 hours when the water is colder than 41 F; a free chlorine residual of at least 0.2 mg/L must still be found at every sample point at the end. Continuous feed (Sec. 4.4): first flush the main at 3.0 ft per second or more, then refill while feeding chlorine for 25 mg/L throughout; hold 24 hours; at least 10 mg/L free chlorine must remain at the end. Slug method (Sec. 4.5): move a slug of water dosed to 100 mg/L slowly down the main so every part of the wall sees it for at least 3 hours; if it falls below 50 mg/L, stop and bring it back to 100. Then flush to normal system chlorine, dechlorinate the flush water before it reaches a drain or stream, and take bacteriological samples. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
chunk.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6 (our summary; facts only)
chunk.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
chunk.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

chunk.title: Bac-T samples on a new water main: two sets, 16 hours, every 1,200 ft (AWWA C651-14)
chunk.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
chunk.text: After final flushing, AWWA C651-14 (Sec. 5.1) requires two sets of bacteriological samples that both pass, taken one of two ways. Option A: take a first set, then take a second set at least 16 hours later. Option B: let the flushed main sit for at least 16 hours with no water use, then take two sets at least 15 minutes apart with the sample taps left running and without flushing the main first. Where to sample: a set for every 1,200 ft of new main, plus one at the end of the line and at least one from each branch longer than one pipe length. If trench water or a lot of dirt got into the main during laying, sample about every 200 ft. If a sample fails: flush and sample again; if it still fails, chlorinate again by the continuous feed or slug method and repeat until both sets pass. Older specs written on the 2005 edition ask for two sets 24 hours apart. No tie-in or service until the agency releases the main. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
chunk.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 5.1.1, 5.1.4, 5.1.6 (our summary; facts only)
chunk.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
chunk.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

chunk.title: Disinfecting a cut-in, repair or final tie-in: 1 percent chlorine swab and the 20 ft rule (AWWA C651-14)
chunk.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
chunk.text: AWWA C651-14 on tie-ins and repairs. Final connection to the existing main (Sec. 4.10): tie-in piping up to one pipe length, generally 20 ft or less, may be sprayed or swabbed inside with at least a 1 percent chlorine solution just before it goes in. A longer connection must be set up above ground, disinfected and pass bacteriological samples before it is installed.
