Repairs (Sec. 4.11): if the main stayed under pressure and the leak was controlled (a clamp on a live main), swab or spray the parts with 1 percent chlorine and flush; no samples are needed. If the main was shut down and depressurized but kept clean: 1 percent chlorine on the exposed pipe, reachable inside surfaces and new parts, flush about three pipe volumes until clear, and take a sample set downstream; it may go back in service before results. If dirty water got in, disinfect like a new main where practical and get passing samples before service. Keep the trench pumped below the pipe while it is open. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
chunk.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 4.10, 4.11, 5.1.2 (our summary; facts only)
chunk.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
chunk.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

chunk.title: Texas construction stormwater permit TXR150000: 1 acre, small and large sites, SWP3
chunk.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
chunk.text: Texas issues its own construction stormwater permit through TCEQ: the Construction General Permit, TXR150000. The current permit took effect March 5, 2023 and "expires on March 5, 2028." It covers construction that discharges stormwater to surface water in the state and will "disturb an acre or more of soil", including smaller sites that are part of a larger common plan. Small sites: "Small construction activities which disturb at least 1 but less than 5 acres" need a stormwater pollution prevention plan (Texas calls it the SWP3) and a signed site notice posted at the site; no Notice of Intent is filed with the state. Large sites: "Large construction activities which disturb 5 or more acres" need the SWP3, a Notice of Intent filed online through STEERS (or with an electronic reporting waiver), and the large-site notices posted. In every case operators must "develop and implement a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWP3) prior to commencing construction." Sites under 1 acre that are not part of a larger plan are "not regulated by this general permit", though the city may have its own rules. TCEQ began work on the 2028 renewal in June 2026.
chunk.source: TCEQ, Stormwater General Permit for Construction Activities (TXR150000), page modified 2026-11-16

chunk.title: California state highway encroachment permit (Caltrans): form TR-0100, CEPS, 60 days
chunk.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
chunk.text: In California, any work in, under or over a state highway right of way needs a Caltrans encroachment permit before it starts: trenches, bores, potholing, driveways, surveys, even tree trimming. The law treats "any tower, pole, pole line, pipe, pipeline, fence, billboard, stand or building" placed in the right of way as an encroachment. How to apply: the Standard Encroachment Permit Application, form TR-0100, with plans and traffic control, goes to the Caltrans district the job is in. Caltrans says "Effective January 1, 2025, you will be required to submit all permit applications through CEPS", its online Encroachment Permit System. Time: under Streets and Highways Code section 671.5, Caltrans must approve or deny a complete application "within 60 calendar days"; an incomplete package restarts the wait. Cost: a deposit at submittal, then actual review and inspection time at the Standard Hourly Rate, $181 per hour effective January 1, 2026. On the job: keep the permit and approved plans on site, call the Caltrans inspector named on the permit before starting, and follow its work hours and lane closure charts. City and county streets need the city or county permit instead.
chunk.source: Caltrans Encroachment Permits program page; Streets and Highways Code 671.5(a); read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Texas state highway utility permit: the TxDOT UIR system and notice of proposed installation
chunk.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
chunk.text: In Texas, putting a utility line in, under or across a state highway right of way goes through TxDOT's Utility Installation Review (UIR) system. TxDOT describes UIR as "a web-based system that automates the submission, review, approval, inspection, and post-construction processing" of "utility installation requests on the state right of way (ROW)". TxDOT calls the request a notice of proposed installation (NOPI). The utility owner, not the pipe contractor, is the applicant: it files the request with plans in UIR, and the TxDOT district reviews and approves it. The rules for where and how a line can go are in TxDOT's Utility Accommodation Rules and its Utility Manual. For the crew: do not start in TxDOT right of way without the approved request in hand; keep a copy on site; give the district office the advance notice the approval calls for; and build what was approved, since changes go back through UIR. Review times and the exact notice period before starting were not confirmed from the TxDOT pages read for this chunk; get them from the approval and the district utility coordinator. County roads and city streets have their own permits.
chunk.source: TxDOT Utility Installation Review (UIR) help pages, About UIR; read 2026-11-20
chunk.unconfirmed: review time and the start-of-work notice period

chunk.title: Florida state road utility permit (FDOT): the Utility Accommodation Manual
chunk.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
chunk.text: In Florida, utility work in a state road right of way needs an FDOT utility permit. Rule 14-46.001 of the state administrative code says its purpose is to "regulate the location and manner for installation and adjustment of utility facilities" on FDOT right of way, and that FDOT issues permits for the "construction, alteration, operation, relocation, removal, and maintenance of utilities." The rule adopts the FDOT Utility Accommodation Manual (UAM), "2017 edition", effective July 30, 2017. FDOT says utilities must be installed "in accordance with the 2017 Utility Accommodation Manual (UAM)", the permit and any agreement with the department. The permit is issued to the utility owner (FDOT calls it the utility/agency owner, UAO); the contractor works under it. For the crew: have the approved permit and plans on site, give the notice before starting that the permit states, and follow the permit's lane closure and restoration conditions. How to file (FDOT's online permitting site) and the review time were not confirmed from the pages read for this chunk; the FDOT district utility office will say. County and city roads have their own right-of-way permits.
chunk.source: Fla. Admin. Code R. 14-46.001 (amended 7/30/2017); FDOT Utilities FAQ; read 2026-11-20
chunk.unconfirmed: how to file online and the review time

chunk.title: Florida bac-T rule for new water mains: two samples on separate days, 6 hours apart
chunk.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
chunk.text: Florida sets its own sampling rule for new and altered public water mains in Rule 62-555.340 of the state administrative code (Department of Environmental Protection). Disinfection must follow "AWWA Standard C651, C652, or C653" (C651 is the one for water mains). Then, at each sampling location, the rule requires "a total of at least two samples - each taken on a separate day and taken at least six hours apart from the other sample(s)". If any sample shows total coliform, sampling goes on "until two consecutive samples at each sampling location show the absence of total coliform." The sampling locations are the ones called for in the AWWA standard (for mains: along the line at set spacing, at the end, and on branches). So in this state the two sets cannot both be pulled the same day, even though the 2014 edition of AWWA C651 has an option for two sets 15 minutes apart after the main sits 16 hours. The main cannot be placed in service until the department or county health unit clears it based on the results. The rule text read was last amended August 28, 2003; check with the permitting office for any newer requirement in the construction permit.
chunk.source: Fla. Admin. Code R. 62-555.340 (amended 8-28-03); read 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Washington trench sloping by soil type (Table N-1): no steeper short-term slope in Type A
chunk.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
chunk.text: Washington's trench sloping table is Table N-1 in WAC 296-155-66403 (Part N, Appendix B). Maximum allowable slopes, horizontal to vertical, for excavations less than 20 ft deep: stable rock vertical (90 degrees); Type A soil 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B soil 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C soil 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Sloping or benching for an excavation deeper than 20 ft must be designed by a registered professional engineer. Where it differs from the federal table: the federal table (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1) has a note allowing a steeper short-term slope of 1/2 to 1 in Type A soil for excavations 12 ft or less that are open 24 hours or less. Table N-1 has no such note and the Washington appendix has no short-term allowance, so on a Washington job Type A is 3/4 to 1 no matter how short a time the trench is open. In the app's Trench Sloping screen, pick plain Type A (0.75:1) on a Washington job; its 'Type A, short-term' choice (0.5:1) is the federal note and is not in Washington's table. The competent person classifies the soil and picks the slope.
chunk.source: WAC 296-155-66403 Table N-1 and notes (WSR 16-09-085); 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Table B-1 note 2

chunk.title: Alabama trench protection depth: the federal OSHA rule, 5 feet (trench box, shoring, sloping)
chunk.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
chunk.text: Alabama has no state OSHA plan that covers private employers, so federal OSHA covers private construction crews there (OSHA list of State Plans). Trench protection: a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench box / shield) is required in an excavation 5 ft or deeper unless it is entirely in stable rock, and in a shallower one when the competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)). There is no separate Alabama trench depth rule for private crews in the library; the competent person decides what protection the trench gets.
chunk.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); OSHA State Plans list (osha.gov/stateplans); app state table checked 2026-11-19
chunk.edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P as in force 2026-11-20

chunk.title: Idaho trench protection depth: the federal OSHA rule, 5 feet (trench box, shoring, sloping)
chunk.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
chunk.text: Idaho has no state OSHA plan that covers private employers, so federal OSHA covers private construction crews there (OSHA list of State Plans). Trench protection: a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench box / shield) is required in an excavation 5 ft or deeper unless it is entirely in stable rock, and in a shallower one when the competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)). There is no separate Idaho trench depth rule for private crews in the library; the competent person decides what protection the trench gets.
chunk.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); OSHA State Plans list (osha.gov/stateplans); app state table checked 2026-11-19
chunk.edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P as in force 2026-11-20
